content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/feniix/.claude/skills/gh-stack

# gh-stack

`gh stack` is a [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) extension for stacked branches and pull
requests. A stack is an ordered chain of branches rooted on a trunk, where each branch has one PR
based on the branch below it, so a reviewer sees only that layer's diff.

`gh stack` prints a stack trunk-first, left to right:

```
(main) <- auth <- api <- frontend
```

Left is the **bottom**, right is the **top**. `auth` is based on `main` and merges first;
`frontend` merges last. `up` moves toward the top, away from trunk; `down` moves toward it.
Foundational work belongs at the bottom, code that depends on it above. For how to choose the
layers, read `references/stack-design.md`.

## Setup

Requires Git 2.36+ and an authenticated GitHub CLI.

```bash
gh extension install github/gh-stack
git config rerere.enabled true         # remember conflict resolutions
git config remote.pushDefault origin   # required if the repo has more than one remote
```

## Non-interactive use

`gh stack` branches on whether **stdout is a TTY**. Piped, most commands error cleanly or print
static text; under a PTY the same commands open a prompt or a full-screen TUI and block forever.
Agent harnesses differ, so always pass the flags below instead of relying on that detection.

**Multiple remotes:** never run `push`, `submit`, `sync`, `rebase`, or `link` without
`--remote <name>` unless `remote.pushDefault` is configured. `checkout` and `trunk` have no
`--remote` flag and require the config.

| Always run | Never run bare | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `gh stack view --json` | `gh stack view` | opens a TUI under a PTY |
| `gh stack submit --auto` | `gh stack submit` | prompts for a title per new PR |
| `gh stack merge <target> --yes` | `gh pr merge` | `gh pr merge` cannot merge a stack |
| `gh stack init <branch>...` | `gh stack init` | prompts for branch names |
| `gh stack add <branch>` | `gh stack add` | prompts for a name, and fails even when piped |
| `gh stack checkout <target>` | `gh stack checkout` | opens a selection menu |
| `gh stack up` / `down` / `top` / `bottom` | `gh stack switch` | `switch` is menu-only |
| — | `gh stack modify` | TUI-only, no non-interactive path |

- `view --short` is safe in both modes, but it is formatted for humans. Use `--json` to parse.
- **`checkout <pr>` when a different local stack already covers those branches** cannot be forced.
  Run `gh stack unstack --local` first (this keeps the stack on GitHub), then retry.
- **Worktrees:** local stacks share one common-directory catalog. Use `--print-path` with
  navigation or explicit-target `checkout` to locate a foreign-owned branch without stealing its
  checkout. Unoccupied targets are checked out here first. Check the exit status before changing
  directories; parse only successful path-mode stdout, never status messages.

## Branch placement

- **Starting multi-part work:** create the stack before writing files. Do not implement every
  concern on trunk and split it later. Put one dependent concern in each layer, bottom to top.
- **Editing an existing stack:** check out the layer that owns the change before editing. Never
  commit a lower layer's concern on the current top branch. Run `gh stack view --json`; if
  ownership is unclear, inspect `git log --all -- <path>`. Then check out the owner, edit, commit,
  rebase upstack, and return to top.

```bash
gh stack down                   # or: gh stack checkout api
git add ... && git commit -m "Add get-user endpoint"
gh stack rebase --upstack       # replay every branch above onto the change
gh stack top                    # return to where you were
gh stack push
```

## Core loop

```bash
gh stack init auth              # create the stack and check out its branch
git add ... && git commit -m "Add auth middleware"
gh stack add api                # next layer, branched from the current one
git add ... && git commit -m "Add API routes"
gh stack submit --auto          # push every branch and open draft PRs
gh stack view --json            # confirm
```

Add `--open` to `submit` to create PRs ready for review instead of drafts. Branch names are
verbatim — `gh stack add refactor/foo` creates `refactor/foo`.

## Staying in sync

```bash
gh stack sync                   # fetch, reconcile with GitHub, rebase, push, refresh PR state
gh stack sync --prune           # also delete local branches for merged PRs
```

Pruning never happens without `--prune` when non-interactive. If the local and remote stacks have
diverged, `sync` prints both chains, makes no changes, and exits 0 with `Sync aborted` — see
`references/troubleshooting.md`.

## Merging

Scope the merge with an argument:

```bash
gh stack merge 42 --yes          # PR #42 plus every unmerged PR below it
gh stack merge 7 --yes           # every unmerged PR in stack #7
gh stack merge 42 --yes --squash # or --merge, --rebase, --merge-method <method>
```

Pass a PR number to merge that PR and every unmerged PR below it, or a stack number to merge every
unmerged PR in that stack. The operation is all-or-nothing: if any PR in that set cannot merge,
none do.

Without a method flag the last-used method is reused. If the base branch uses a merge queue, the
stack is queued instead and the queue picks the method, ignoring any flag you passed with a
warning; queued PRs may land in separate groups.

## Reading state

`gh stack view --json` writes JSON to **stdout**. Status messages go to **stderr** — do not parse
them, branch on exit codes instead.

```
trunk           string
currentBranch   string
branches[]      name, head, base, isCurrent, isMerged, isQueued, needsRebase
branches[].pr   number, url, state ("OPEN" | "MERGED" | "QUEUED"); absent when no PR exists
```

`base` is the saved SHA of the parent branch that this branch was last known to contain. It may be
older than the parent's current tip. `needsRebase` is true when the current parent tip is no longer
an ancestor of the branch.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Success | — |
| 1 | Generic error | Read stderr |
| 2 | Not in a stack | `gh stack init`, or `gh stack checkout <target>` |
| 3 | Rebase conflict | Follow the Exit 3 recovery below |
| 4 | GitHub API failure | Check `gh auth status`, retry |
| 5 | Invalid arguments | Fix the invocation; see `<command> --help` |
| 6 | Disambiguation required | Branch is in several stacks; check out a non-shared branch |
| 7 | Rebase already in progress | `gh stack rebase --continue` or `--abort` |
| 8 | Stack file locked | Another `gh stack` process is writing; retry after ~5s |
| 9 | Stacked PRs unavailable | Not enabled on the repository; tell the user |
| 10 | Modify recovery required | `gh stack modify --abort` |

**Exit 3 recovery:**

- After `gh stack rebase`: resolve the files, run `git add`, then
  `gh stack rebase --continue`; use `gh stack rebase --abort` to restore the stack.
- After `gh stack sync`: the stack has already been restored. Run `gh stack rebase` to recreate the
  conflict, then resolve and continue as above.

## Constraints

  affected clean owners; unoccupied branches use the origin. Drop/fold source branches and
  worktrees are preserved. Recovery flags may run from any worktree and use recorded native
  operation owners; never resolve/stage in the caller's tree unless the diagnostic names it.
- There is no non-interactive reorder or removal. Errors may suggest `gh stack modify`, but it is
  TUI-only — restructure with `unstack` then `init` instead.
- PR titles and bodies are auto-generated. Use `gh pr edit` afterwards to change them.

result.output:
# Designing a stack

How to decide what goes in each layer. Read this before running `gh stack init`.

## Contents

- [Plan the layers before writing code](#plan-the-layers-before-writing-code)
- [Branch naming](#branch-naming)
- [Staging changes deliberately](#staging-changes-deliberately)
- [When to add a layer](#when-to-add-a-layer)
- [One stack, one story](#one-stack-one-story)

## Plan the layers before writing code

A stack is a dependency chain. If code in one layer depends on code in another, the dependency must
live in the same branch or a lower one. That constraint is much cheaper to satisfy by planning than
by restructuring later, because there is no non-interactive in-place reorder — fixing the order
means`unstack` and `init` again.

Decide the layers first, then write code into them:

```
(main) <- todo-app/models <- todo-app/api <- todo-app/frontend <- todo-app/integration
```

- `todo-app/models` — shared types and schema
- `todo-app/api` — routes that use the models
- `todo-app/frontend` — components that call the routes
- `todo-app/integration` — tests exercising the whole feature

This is illustrative. Infer the stack topic and layer names from the actual task; do not reuse
`todo-app` or these layer names literally.

The failure mode to avoid is writing everything on one branch and trying to split it afterwards.
If a task is large enough to warrant a stack, create the stack at the start.

## Branch naming

Prefer a shared topic prefix plus the layer's concern:
`<topic>/<concern>` — for example, `billing/schema`, `billing/api`, `billing/ui`.
This keeps related branches recognizable without using generic names that could belong to any
stack. **User and repository branch naming conventions take precedence; follow them instead.**

Names are used exactly as given — nothing is prepended or transformed, and slashes are kept, so
`gh stack add refactor/foo` creates a branch literally named `refactor/foo`.

If you pass `-m` without a branch name, the name is generated from the commit message in
date-and-slug form (for example `03-24-add_api_routes`). Prefer naming the branch yourself.

## Staging changes deliberately

Use `git add` and `git commit` directly rather than the `add -Am` shortcut. The point is control
over which changes land in which branch. With several modified files in the working tree, stage the
subset that belongs to the current layer, commit it, then create the next branch and stage the rest
there:

```bash
git add internal/models/user.go internal/models/session.go
git commit -m "Add user and session models"

gh stack add api-routes
git add internal/api/routes.go internal/api/handlers.go
git commit -m "Add user API routes"
```

Multiple commits per branch are fine. What matters is that every commit in a branch serves the same
concern, and that a change belonging to a different concern goes in a different branch.

Note that `gh stack add <branch>` without `-Am` does not touch the working tree, so uncommitted
changes carry over to the new branch. Commit or stash first if you want the new layer to start clean.

## When to add a layer

Add a branch when you start a **different concern that depends on what you have built so far**.
Signals:

- Moving from backend to frontend, or from core logic to tests or documentation
- The next changes have a different reviewer audience
- The current branch's diff is already large enough to review on its own

A layer that cannot be described in one sentence is usually two layers.

## One stack, one story

A stack should read as a coherent progression: a reviewer walks the PRs bottom to top and sees the
feature being built.

**Use a single stack** when every branch serves the same feature or project, even if the layers span
different concerns.

**Start a separate stack** for unrelated work — a different feature, an unrelated bug fix, an
independent refactor. Do not mix efforts into one stack just because you happened to work on both.
Use `gh stack init` for the new effort, or `gh stack checkout <target>` to move between existing
stacks.

A trivial incidental fix can ride along in the current stack. Once it grows into its own project, it
deserves its own stack.

behavior. MCP retains the portable planner/research contract, not cycle state.
This document maps implementation regressions, not paid production evidence.

The representative test is **“qualifies a complete offline Pi cycle through
curation, final gaps, restart and archival inspection”** in

  and separate-process crash reproduction are not power-loss certification.
- MCP construction/delegation is tested in process; MCP wire-protocol round-trip
  qualification is not claimed.
- Atomic local intents/one-use guards prevent local duplicate authorization;
  they do not create server idempotency or a distributed transaction with Exa.
  Cross-process visibility begins at durable publication of genuine outcomes.
- Private structural historical proofs preserve then-current grants/ledger and
  legitimate later outcomes; they are not cryptographic protection against
  coherent privileged rewriting of all private state.
- SDK receipts are API-reported costs, not verified invoices. Estimates,
  provisional totals, unknown operations, assessed liabilities and overspend
  remain separate. A healthy overview/readiness flag grants no consent.
- Final reports preserve recorded gaps and proposed dispositions, even when a
  valid generated task output claims satisfaction. Completed plans remain
  immutable; evaluation belongs in the final answer, not an automatic plan edit.
  Criterion diagnostics match each view's evidence scope: status uses all recorded
  sources, while brief/source-pack summaries recompute against selected sources
  without changing saved coverage or buying further research.
- Locked/unreadable/legacy stores fail closed for continuation attribution.
  Discovery exposes only coarse unreadable IDs; unrelated explicit standalone
  work remains available. Offline repair must preserve history and live owners.
- Cycle `max`/`ultra`, MCP cycle parity, automatic billing verification and
  production/live paid smoke remain outside this rollout.

## Revalidation

Run frozen-lockfile installation, workspace checks/tests/audit, package coverage,
MCP build and diff checks. Apply fresh read-only source/diff review and current-head
CI before merge. Dependency audit is a separate gate, not implied by green tests.
Root patched transitive overrides clear the previously recorded advisories while
preserving the frozen Pi/Exa/bridgekit versions; rerun audit rather than infer
future safety from that historical result. No merge or release is performed by
qualification.

8	# Pi-first integrated research-cycle contract
9	
10	Sources: [PRD-010](../prd/PRD-010-pi-exa-integrated-research-cycle.md),
11	[feasibility and Jev evidence](../research/pi-exa-integrated-cycle-feasibility.md),
12	[issue #152](https://github.com/feniix/pi-extensions/issues/152).
13	Current source implements the merged v1.2 safety foundation, with an
14	[offline qualification/acceptance map](pi-exa-cycle-qualification.md).
15	Operator choices and delegated Jev selections are design evidence, not runtime
16	consent. PRD-010 v1.3 requires a guided background workflow before 6.1.0 is
17	published. The section below supersedes the foundation's manual normal-path
18	commands and submit-and-poll cycle execution. Later sections describe the
19	reusable foundation and historical slice decisions, not proof of new UX support.
20	
21	## 6.1.0 target: separate proposal, submission, observation and delivery
22	
23	### Boundaries
24	
25	- **Planner/proposal:** assistant-operated non-spending start/update/preview.
26	  Guided intent routes explicitly to its cycle, with no standalone fallback.
27	  A human-readable proposal references the canonical request hash/revision
28	  internally; no second compiler or model-generated authorization object.
29	- **Approval adapter:** actual trusted host response creates durable scoped
30	  grants paired to that proposal. Reuse accounting/request/risk checks, without
31	  asking the user to copy hashes. Cancellation/unavailable UI/stale response
32	  fails closed. A conversational user request starts planning, not spending.
33	- **Submitter:** durable frozen intent and exclusive one-use create claim;
34	  one bounded create wait, remote-ID publication, monitor registration, then
35	  immediate acknowledgement. It does not wait for terminal completion.
36	- **Monitor:** host-owned lifecycle service with bounded same-ID GETs, no model
37	  polling loop, no create/continuation/replacement/cancel authority.
38	- **Reporter/delivery adapter:** terminal receipt and local processing precede
39	  durable notification scheduling. Wake the originating assistant at a safe
40	  turn boundary with an attempt reference, not raw vendor content as instructions.
41	  Reporting is read-only with respect to research spending.
42	
43	Names above are architectural responsibilities, not settled public API names.
44	Do not implement by detaching an untracked promise from the existing blocking
45	tool or by telling the assistant to call that tool repeatedly.
46	
47	### Reuse and changed behavior
48	
49	Preserve the existing canonical project identity, private store, schema checks,
50	curated artifact/result policy, exact grants, monetary arithmetic, final dispatch
51	guards, late-observation accounting and immutable historical consent proofs.
52	Keep remote lifecycle, local processing, local monitoring and notice delivery as
53	separate state dimensions; a stopped monitor is not a failed Agent run.
54	
55	Existing cycle submission currently inherits the shared wait/poll behavior.
56	The redesigned Pi path must not inherit cancellation-on-chat-interruption from
57	the blocking standalone path. Standalone/default-opt-out/MCP retain that
58	existing contract. Explicit recovery remains one bounded saved-run GET; it is
59	not the repeating monitor and must share safe observation coordination.
60	
61	### Monitor ownership and persistence
62	
63	Persist monitor intent bound to canonical project, cycle, attempt, saved remote
64	ID and originating session. Runtime ownership/generation fences permit at most
65	one authorized monitor per attempt across contenders. Use existing proven-dead
66	owner recovery principles, not age alone as takeover authority.
67	
68	Keep network waits outside storage locks. Late genuine responses can settle only
69	their original attempt after detach/archive; stale callbacks cannot re-register
70	timers, notify a different session or submit work. Coalesce unchanged snapshots
71	without losing durability retries, changed costs, conflicts or late success.
72	Repeated explicit status/recovery must not spawn parallel polling loops.
73	
74	Submission and monitor registration can fail independently. If create succeeded
75	but scheduling failed, retain and return the saved ID with “monitoring paused,”
76	not successful monitoring or submission failure. Bounded submission timeout
77	without an ID retains unknown intent. Late acknowledgement is persisted; attach
78	monitoring only if the originating ownership/context remains eligible.
79	
80	Use bounded per-GET deadlines, non-overlapping checks and backoff; honor server
81	retry guidance when available. Numerical cadence/error limits are a design gate.
82	Auth/not-found/exhausted errors pause observation; remote outcome and financial
83	liability remain separate. No background action consumes replacement consent.
84	
85	Shutdown stops local work; restart discovers resumable records without implicit
86	ownership or monitoring. Explicit user-requested assistant resume reacquires the
87	cycle and eligible monitor. Switch/fork/tree/archive fences local monitoring and
88	delivery; explain the pause. This is an in-process Pi feature, not an always-on
89	OS daemon or a promise of notifications after Pi exits.
90	
91	### Durable completion delivery
92	
93	Maintain a durable notice identity per attempt/terminal outcome, with originating
94	session, pending/delivered state and host acknowledgement when supported.
95	Persist the outcome first, then schedule delivery; record failure independently
96	from remote completion. Ordinary duplicate observations enqueue one notice.
97	Late additional financial facts update the record rather than erase the first
98	completion; separately material duplicate success remains reportable.
99	
100	Do not hold the submission tool open or interrupt an active assistant response.
101	Deliver at a safe boundary or wake the idle origin session. For an unavailable/
102	detached origin, retain pending state for explicit resume; never redirect to the
103	currently active unrelated session. Check ownership again at actual delivery.
104	
105	There is no assumed atomic transaction between filesystem publication and Pi
106	message delivery. Validate host acknowledgement semantics before choosing an
107	outbox protocol. Where acknowledgement is ambiguous across crash/restart,
108	surface pending/uncertain delivery and reconcile rather than claim exactly-once.
109	Completion of local processing/reporting is not evidence of criterion coverage.
110	
111	### Implementation gates and verification
112	
113	Before choosing tool schemas or scheduling APIs, inspect the pinned and supported
114	Pi extension APIs/examples for trusted confirmation, nonblocking host lifecycle,
115	safe-turn wakeup, session targeting and message acknowledgements. Verify Exa's
116	create/GET behavior without assuming SDK request abort or server idempotency.
117	Record capability evidence and limitations; reopen the design if a requirement
118	cannot be met. No new runtime dependency or model judgement service is implied.
119	
120	Test first at real registered Pi tools/commands, host confirmation/lifecycle
121	boundaries, private filesystem controllers and mocked Exa endpoints. Use a
122	controllable pending job: submission must finish while the job is still pending,
123	a second user turn must remain possible, and terminal transition must cause
124	one safe completion delivery. Cover crash/fault injection, simultaneous runs,
125	ownership transfer, stale approval, unknown create and missed/ambiguous notices.
126	Finish with an interactive Pi smoke, not merely scripted callback invocation.
127	PRD scenarios 21–36 are the new release gates; old qualification does not satisfy
128	them. Live paid testing and publication require separate authority.
129	
130	## Activation and host separation
131	
132	Pi-only `--exa-enable-cycles` is initially disabled by default. When enabled,
133	an explicitly started/resumed cycle integrates automatically. Planning,
134	compilation, scoped accounting, one-use submission, explicit existing-run
135	recovery and funded retry/replacement are active under that opt-in. Unsupported
136	paths fail closed rather than silently falling back to standalone.
137	Completed-cycle views report recorded gaps/criteria and classified usage without
138	automatic satisfaction, verified billing or follow-up spending. Existing
139	standalone/MCP defaults and tool enablement remain unchanged.
140	
141	Use a thin Pi registration/execution decorator to capture host context.
142	Inject optional host-neutral per-call raw-response/lifecycle observers into shared
143	helpers/factory, including late responses and cancel replies. MCP does not install
144	cycle behavior. Never use process-global mutable current-call context under concurrency.

146	## Identity, ownership, and durability
147	
148	Project identity hashes canonical Git common directory, or canonical cwd outside
149	Git. Cycles have generated IDs, schema versions, monotonic plan revisions and
150	separate attempt IDs. Owner identity combines Pi session ID and runtime token.
151	Store curated JSON under the configured Pi agent directory's
152	`research-cycles/<project-id>/`, with restrictive directory/file permissions.
153	
154	Start/switch/fork/clone/tree navigation/reload detaches the active pointer.
155	Explicit resume acquires exclusive ownership; a live owner blocks takeover.
156	Dead-owner recovery needs verified local liveness or explicit operator recovery,
157	not TTL alone. Unknown remote execution remains unknown after stale-owner recovery.
158	Old callbacks may reconcile their attempt under lock, but cannot submit more work
159	or overwrite another owner's plan. Compaction does not rewind durable state.
160	
161	Short cross-process locks cover complete read/validate/reserve/durable-write
162	transactions, not network waits. Write/sync a same-directory temporary record,
163	atomically replace and sync its directory before submission. Outstanding durable
164	attempts and fenced ownership prevent duplicate automatic submissions.
165	Fail closed where filesystem durability/locking is unsupported.
166	Storage implementation chooses platform primitives and tests crash points;
167	it must not weaken the invariants.
168	
169	Reset/archive detaches, retaining attempts, accounting, grants and liabilities.
170	It never cancels remote work or makes completed records executable.
171	Permanent deletion is outside this release.

173	## Commands and spending grants

175	- `/exa-research start <topic>` creates/activates without paid work.

449	both results/charges survive, status and late progress surface duplicate
450	successes, and completion blocks a third call. Malformed/stale/underfunded risk
451	commands leave grants unchanged and never dispatch. Default-opt-out/standalone/
452	MCP behavior is unchanged. Full-feature review/publication remains pending.
453	
454	## #158 delegated recovery decisions
455	
456	Jev selected explicit Pi-only actions on existing tools: status `action=resume`
457	with a saved cycle ID, and Agent `researchMode=recover` for the existing
458	attempt. Default status remains inspection; neither startup nor saved-state
459	discovery implicitly resumes or grants spending consent. Standalone/MCP
460	contracts remain unchanged.
461	
462	Recovery is one bounded SDK `agent.runs.get(id)` per explicit invocation, not
463	`create(previousRunId)`, an automatic polling loop or remote cancellation.
464	Local timeout/abort leaves the original attempt outcome uncertain; attached
465	call-local observers may still reconcile a late genuine reply. Missing IDs,
466	404/auth/network failures remain actionable unknown, not fabricated remote
467	failure. GET must bind the original saved attempt and validate/reprocess with
468	its frozen artifact/schema, without a new operation, grant or submission.
469	Source: Exa get-a-run primary documentation and pinned SDK 2.23.0.
470	Evidence: `/tmp/pi-exa-158-jev-{request,response}.json`.
471	
472	The SDK inspection, original-attempt controller and registered Pi tool slices
473	are now implemented with offline regressions. Pi status discovers saved
474	summaries without activation; explicit resume acquires ownership, and explicit
475	Agent recovery performs one GET without a new attempt/reservation. Missing IDs
476	stay unknown, terminal completion cannot be undone, frozen assertions are
477	checked at preparation and actual GET preparation, and each GET observation
478	capability is one-use. Provider prose/raw responses remain outside durable
479	storage. The complete layer still requires fresh full-diff review; replacement
480	and whole-workflow rollout remain #159/#160.
481	
482	## #157 review decisions
483	
484	Fresh full-diff review identified two non-blocking display/diagnostic gaps.
485	Under the operator's delegated design authority, Jev selected a neutral
486	assessment-only `ledgerHealthy` status field (never a status `canDispatch`
487	claim) and a closed, package-owned remote-error summary instead of archiving
488	arbitrary vendor prose. Real per-request assessments retain `canDispatch`.
489	Evidence: `/tmp/pi-exa-157-jev-review-{request,response}.json`.
490	
491	## #156 evidence implementation decisions
492	
493	The operator approved metadata-first candidate retention and the public testing
494	seams: candidate normalization/curation policy, the real-filesystem cycle
495	controller, and registered Pi tools with mocked SDK responses/compiler previews.
496	
497	Cycle-attributed retrievals retain only stable candidate identities, bounded
498	titles/URLs, retrieval state and operation-bound provenance. Source bodies,
499	highlights, summaries, generated answers, processing rows and full SDK responses
500	are not automatically retained. Useful content notes are explicit curation.
501	Candidate capture does not select evidence or satisfy criteria.
502	
503	Candidate selection/rejection is an explicit planning update. Selection records
504	a planner source and a labeled execution-plan evidence reference; rejection
505	removes that candidate's selection without erasing its provenance. Existing
506	explicit source updates remain the external-evidence interface. Only selected
507	source facts and provenance enter previews; input rows remain explicit.
508	
509	Automatic capture requires the original active planning cycle and runtime
510	ownership. Detach/archive/ownership change prevents delayed callbacks from
511	changing evidence; late accounting remains a separate operation-bound capability.
512	The generation fence and final candidate namespace replacement are one synchronous
513	publication step under the filesystem lock. Revocation during asynchronous
514	preparation prevents publication; revocation after replacement does not undo
515	the already-published capture. File/directory synchronization remains required.
516	Candidate metadata is backward-compatible optional durable state, not a raw
517	response archive. Standalone, default opt-out and MCP calls do not capture it.
518	
519	## #155 accounting design grill
520	
521	The operator approved the accounting-policy, real-filesystem controller, and
522	registered Pi command/tool testing seams. Design-time Jev (`jev-1.13.0`) selected
523	the following choices in dependency-aware rounds; the operator confirmed the
524	resulting design before implementation. Jev is not a runtime dependency.
525	
526	- Approval amounts set a **total lifetime ceiling**, never additive credits.
527	- Call-local shared-tool factories carry operation-bound raw/late SDK observers.
528	- Default grants cover an explicit supported exploratory retrieval allowlist,
529	  not Agent, Connect/contact work or unknown extras.
530	- Package-owned published-price profiles record source, publication/review date,
531	  version and request-derived basis. They are estimates, not vendor billing caps
532	  or invoice verification. Unsupported pricing fails closed without a separately
533	  approved, immutable-request-bound uncertainty assessment.
534	- Checked integer micro-USD arithmetic rounds permission down and exposure up;
535	  invalid inputs and sum overflow fail closed.
536	- Owned, atomic assessments count reported usage, all pending estimates and
537	  explicitly assessed unknown liabilities. Durable operation identity/request
538	  hash and reservation precede SDK invocation; network waits never hold locks.
539	- Interrupted reservations remain possible liabilities. Unknown cost blocks
540	  autonomous spending until a valid receipt or operator permission naming that
541	  exact operation and assessed liability allowance. Permission does not change
542	  its classification to reported cost or cover future unknown operations.
543	- Genuine late callbacks reconcile only their saved operation, including after
544	  detach/archive/ownership changes. They cannot mutate plans, owners, lifecycle,
545	  grants or submission eligibility.
546	- Amendments preserve history and apply the latest ceiling/scope to new work;
547	  insufficient balance and overspend are surfaced before further dispatch.
548	- Only explicit valid API totals, including zero, resolve to API-reported usage.
549	  Reservations are replaced once; components are not counted again. Missing or
550	  malformed totals remain unknown. Conflicting receipts remain auditable and
551	  block new work rather than silently applying last-write-wins. Local formatting
552	  failures cannot discard genuine usage receipts.
553	- Versioned accounting records validate identities, money, scope and uniqueness.
554	  Opaque legacy data is preserved, never inferred as consent or zero liability.
555	- Release a reservation only when call-local facts prove SDK invocation never
556	  occurred. A local timeout, cancellation or error flag alone is insufficient.
557	
558	The 12 grill selections had selected-option probabilities 0.97–1.00; this is
559	design evidence, not proof of correctness. Offline regressions and independent
560	adversarial review remain required. Development approval grants no live spending.

result.output:
# Changelog

All notable changes to `@feniix/pi-exa` are recorded in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

Entries before 5.0.0 are reconstructed from package-scoped Git history and npm
publication metadata. Dates are npm publication dates (UTC); early manifest and
publication version mismatches are called out explicitly.

## [Unreleased]

### Added

- **Opt-in integrated Pi research cycles** behind `--exa-enable-cycles`, disabled by default. Explicit start/resume connects planning, curated evidence, request previews, approved research, results and accounting. `/exa-research` manages project-isolated durable cycles; session navigation/reload detaches ownership, and reset archives history rather than deleting it or cancelling remote work.
- **Versioned, immutable Agent request artifacts** compiled from curated goals, criteria, scope, constraints, selected evidence and a draft-07 structured task contract. Preview and execution share the authoritative request; stale references, conflicting overrides and unsupported schemas fail closed. Explicit input/exclusion rows remain separate from selected source context.
- **Operator-issued lifetime ceilings and scoped, one-use permissions.** Exploratory calls reserve exposure before dispatch; Agent research additionally requires an exact full-request assessment. Unknown liabilities, pending estimates, API-reported receipts and overspend are classified separately. Assistant flags, readiness, healthy accounting and supplied amounts never establish spending consent.
- **Metadata-first evidence candidates** from cycle-attributed retrievals, with stable URL identities, retrieval state and operation provenance. Selection/rejection and candidate/external-source curation are explicit; only selected source context enters compiled requests and brief/source-pack summaries. Discovery never automatically selects evidence or satisfies criteria.
- **Durable Agent submission intent and one-use dispatch claims**, with final ownership, generation, request, history and funding checks before SDK create. Curated results retain validated task output, safe citation metadata, usage and package-owned diagnostics. Genuine late outcomes reconcile their original attempts, including after archival; remote success closes the cycle even when local processing fails.
- **Explicit saved-cycle resume and existing-run recovery** through status `action: "resume"` and Agent `researchMode: "recover"`. Recovery performs one bounded GET against the saved run and original frozen contract, without a new submission, reservation, polling loop or remote cancellation. Missing IDs and unavailable inspection preserve unknown work.
- **Explicitly funded retry and replacement** through Agent `researchMode: "retry"` / `"replace"`. Each new attempt needs fresh exact-request funding; every unknown original additionally needs operator `approve-replacement` acknowledging duplicate work and possible additional charges. Historical contracts, consumed permissions and liabilities remain intact; genuine completion blocks further submissions and duplicate successes remain visible.
- **Read-only final cycle reports** with recorded criteria, evidence-reference diagnostics, gaps, assumptions, completion facts and classified usage. Integrated tool guidance and the planner skill describe the Pi workflow; the offline qualification document maps all 20 PRD-010 acceptance scenarios.

### Changed

- **Coalesce unchanged Agent observations and reuse status projections**, avoiding redundant record rewrites and repeated storage-hierarchy synchronization while preserving changed/late usage, results, conflicting receipts and durability repair.
- Add `ajv` and `ajv-formats` for synchronous local draft-07 task/result validation; validation does not fetch remote schemas.
- Standalone/default-opt-out/MCP behavior and existing tool enablement remain unchanged. Cycle `max`/`ultra` and MCP cycle parity remain outside this rollout. SDK receipts are not independently verified invoices; estimates and lifetime ceilings are not vendor billing caps.

### Fixed

- **Replacement liability guards reuse the complete shared attempt floor**, including known receipt conflicts and the immutable fixed-effort base, instead of re-deriving a partial floor. Stale replacement consent is rejected before reservation without consuming permissions or changing saved history.
- **Exact conservative decimal micro-USD conversion** avoids binary floating-point boundary errors when flooring permission or ceiling exposure. Equivalent known terminal SDK receipts retain legitimate historical rounding without creating false conflicts; genuinely changed receipts remain auditable.
- **Storage and ownership availability:** atomically published PID/token transaction locks recover only proven-dead owners, use monotonic bounded contention waits and clean candidate links. Unverifiable/live locks are retained with actionable repair paths. Archiving unrelated history no longer revokes the active cycle, and readable discovery survives corrupt records while continuation attribution stays fail-closed.
- **Standalone isolation and selected-only summaries:** explicit unrelated standalone retrieval bypasses owned-cycle status failures without bypassing saved-run attribution. Shared summary projection prevents drift, and final-report diagnostics match the evidence visible in each view without changing saved criteria or exposing unselected source notes.

### Security

- Keep durable cycle state private and outside git. Automatic retention excludes raw source bodies, full SDK responses, invalid generated output and arbitrary vendor error prose; credential-bearing/signed URLs and Agent path dot segments are rejected. Explicit curated notes/rows and requested structured task outputs must remain nonsecret.
- Patch shared transitive dependencies through workspace overrides: `proxy-addr` 2.0.8, `source-map-js` 1.2.2 and `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.31.0. This clears the recorded dependency advisories without changing the frozen Pi, Exa or bridgekit versions.

## [6.0.2] - 2026-10-06

### Changed

- Align shared CI and release tooling with Pi upstream's Node 22 runtime and typings.
- Validate the extension and MCP build on Node.js 22.19.0 and the latest Node 22; the existing Node.js minimum and Exa runtime behavior are unchanged.

result.output: # Extensions Extensions are TypeScript modules that add executable behavior to Pi. Use one when a workflow needs tools, commands, event handlers, model providers, session state, or terminal UI rather than instructions alone. An extension runs inside the Pi process with the same operating-system permissions. It can inspect prompts, tool calls, files, credentials, and session history, so load extensions only from sources you trust. Typical extensions add an agent tool, protect paths, confirm dangerous commands, react to session events, modify context, expose a command, or display persistent status. ## Create and load an extension An extension exports a default factory that receives `ExtensionAPI`. The factory registers capabilities for the current extension runtime. Create `~/.pi/agent/extensions/hello.ts`: ```typescript import type { ExtensionAPI } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent"; export default function (pi: ExtensionAPI) { pi.registerCommand("hello", { description: "Show a greeting", handler: async (name, ctx) => { ctx.ui.notify(`Hello, ${name || "world"}!`, "info"); }, }); } ``` Start Pi and run `/hello`. During development, load a file directly: ```bash pi --extension ./hello.ts ``` Pi uses `jiti`, so local TypeScript extensions do not need a separate compilation step. Use [Pi packages](packages.md) for distributed extensions and dependencies. ## Add it to Pi Place the extension in your user or project extensions directory. Pi loads direct TypeScript or JavaScript files and subdirectories containing an `index.ts` or `index.js` entry point. Use a single file for a small extension and a directory for a multi-file implementation. Put npm dependencies in a nearby `package.json`. See [Configuration](configuration.md) for conventional locations and [Settings](settings.md#resources) for additional paths. Reload replaces the extension runtime, so code after `await ctx.reload()` must not reuse state from the old runtime. Only personal and explicit command-line extensions can participate in the `project_trust` event that runs before project extensions load. ## Respect the runtime lifecycle The factory can be synchronous or asynchronous. Pi waits for an asynchronous factory before startup continues, allowing it to fetch configuration or register providers needed during startup. Do not start processes, sockets, watchers, or timers in the factory because some invocations load extensions without starting a session. Start long-lived resources from `session_start` or from the command or tool that needs them. Close session-scoped resources from an idempotent `session_shutdown` handler. A run proceeds from input and `before_agent_start`, through model, message, and tool events, to `agent_end`. Automatic retries, recovery, compaction, or queued work can continue afterward. `agent_before_settle` is the final actionable boundary: it can append entries and request one continuation. `agent_settled` is final and notification-only; use it when an integration needs to know Pi will not continue automatically. ## Choose an integration point | Capability | Main API | |---|---| | Observe or modify lifecycle behavior | `pi.on()` | | Add a model-callable operation | `pi.registerTool()` | | Add a `/` command | `pi.registerCommand()` | | Add a shortcut or CLI flag | `pi.registerShortcut()` or `pi.registerFlag()` | | Send user or custom messages | `pi.sendUserMessage()` or `pi.sendMessage()` | | Persist non-context session data | `pi.appendEntry()` | | Change active tools, model, or thinking level | Session control methods on `pi` | | Add a model provider | `pi.registerProvider()` | | Add an MCP server | `pi.registerMcpServer()` | | Route each request to a model | [`pi.registerVirtualModel()`](virtual-models.md) | | Add terminal rendering | Renderer registration and `ctx.ui` | | Communicate with another extension | `pi.events` | Use the exported declarations in [`extensions/types.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/extensions/types.ts) for exact event, context, tool, and result types. ## Follow the extension contracts ### Events and concurrency Handlers run in extension load and registration order. `pi.on()` returns a function that unsubscribes that registration; changes do not affect a dispatch already in progress. Some events notify; others transform data, replace results, or cancel an operation. Use each event’s declared result type rather than assuming every return value has an effect. Events cover resource discovery, sessions, agent and message lifecycle, providers, tools, and raw input. `before_agent_start` exposes both the current prompt and its structured `systemPromptOptions`. Prefer changing prompt sections, selected tools, or guidelines so Pi can append a transcript delta. Returning `systemPrompt`, or setting `forceSystemPrompt`, replaces the whole prompt for that run while the transcript continues recording the structured sections. Providers receive the forced text as their leading system prompt. `message_end` can replace a finalized message while preserving its role. `tool_call` can mutate input or block execution. `tool_result` handlers compose, with each handler seeing prior changes. `provider_stream_event` fires for each parsed provider stream event before Pi normalizes it. The event identifies the provider, API, and model; `event.data` is the earliest structured value available to Pi, not necessarily the original HTTP bytes or SSE frame. Treat it as read-only because mutation can affect normalization. The event is notification-only and is not persisted. Handlers are awaited in stream order, so slow handlers delay stream consumption. Handler errors are reported without changing the provider response. See [`debug-provider.ts`](../examples/extensions/debug-provider.ts) for an opt-in viewer that groups raw events by assistant message. `context` transforms conversation messages without prompt and tool system messages; Pi restores that state afterward. Use `context_with_system` only when a request-local transformation must own the complete transcript, and keep a system message at index zero. `turn_end` and `agent_before_settle` are actionable boundaries. Their handlers can chain proposed `custom`, `custom_message`, `context_edit`, or `compaction` entries and return `continue: true` for one next model request. Guard continuation conditions because an unconditional continuation can loop. Use the exported event declarations for the complete validation and ordering contract. `cache_warming_decision` can override an idle prompt-cache refresh with `{ action: "warm" }` or `{ action: "stop" }`. The last handler that returns an action wins. Tool calls from one assistant message can run in parallel. Do not assume a sibling call or result exists when another tool event runs. Use `ctx.signal` for nested work owned by an active turn; commands and idle session events often have no operation signal. A `user_bash` handler that returns `undefined` passes the command to the next handler and then to local execution if no handler handles it. Returning `operations` or `result` stops propagation. A handler failure blocks the command rather than falling through to local execution. ### Tools A custom tool defines a name, model-facing description, TypeBox parameter schema, and `execute()` function. Its result requires model-facing `content` and a `details` field for rendering or state reconstruction. Use `details: undefined` when there are no structured details. If the tool makes nested model calls, include their `usage` in the result so session totals remain accurate. Throw from `execute()` to produce a failed tool result. Returning an object does not mark it as an error. Return `terminate: true` only when the agent should skip its automatic follow-up after every completed tool in that batch agrees to terminate. Use sequential execution when tools share mutable in-memory state. File-mutating tools should wrap the complete read-modify-write operation with `withFileMutationQueue()`. Truncate large model-facing results and tell the model where to read the complete output. Declare `outputSchema` and return a matching `structuredContent` when the result is data. The model still receives `content`; programmatic callers such as codemode scripts receive `structuredContent` instead of the text. Tools without `outputSchema` are passed to scripts as their text content. To report a failure that still carries data, return the result with `isError: true` instead of throwing: the model sees an error, and scripts still receive `structuredContent`. A tool can run other tools with `ctx.executeTool(name, args, { signal, onUpdate })`. Nested calls go through argument validation and the `tool_call` and `tool_result` handlers like model-issued calls, and emit `tool_execution_start`, `tool_execution_update`, and `tool_execution_end`; all of these events carry `parentToolCallId`, and their `toolCallId` is assigned by pi as `/`. These ids do not appear as tool calls or tool results in the transcript. Nested calls do not add transcript entries: their results only reach the calling tool, which reports them itself, for example through `onUpdate` and `details`. The session keeps a bounded record of them (name, arguments, status, duration, error; never results) as `nestedCalls` on the calling tool's result message. It is used for compaction file lists and shown in HTML exports. Arguments over 8 KiB per call or 32 KiB per tool result are omitted, at most 256 calls are kept, and `complete: false` marks a record that lost anything. The `usage` of nested results, at every depth, is added to the calling tool's result `usage`, so a tool reports only its own usage, not that of the tools it called. `ctx.tools` lists the tools `ctx.executeTool()` can call. `tool_result` handlers that redact `content` should also replace `structuredContent`; replacing only `content` drops it. See [`hello.ts`](../examples/extensions/hello.ts), [`todo.ts`](../examples/extensions/todo.ts), [`dynamic-tools.ts`](../examples/extensions/dynamic-tools.ts), and [`truncated-tool.ts`](../examples/extensions/truncated-tool.ts). ### Tool exposure `exposure` controls how the model reaches a tool. "Callable" means callable from other tools through `ctx.executeTool()` (`ctx.tools`), as the `codemode` tool's scripts do: - `direct` (default): declared to the model while active, and callable while active. - `model-only`: declared to the model while active, never callable. Use it for tools that orchestrate other tools or ask the user. - `codemode`: callable whenever registered, and listed by the `codemode` tool. Not declared to the model unless activated explicitly. - `deferred`: like `codemode`, but codemode tools do not list it; `tool_search` can find and activate it. - `hidden`: registered but unreachable. Re-register a tool with `exposure: "hidden"` to withdraw it, since tools cannot be unregistered. `namespace: { name, description, instructions }` groups related tools, as MCP servers do. Codemode tools list a namespace under one heading with its `description`. `instructions` holds longer usage guidance; it is not listed, and codemode scripts read it with `describeNamespace(name)`. Registering a `direct` or `model-only` tool activates it; the other exposures are not activated on registration. The active set (`pi.getActiveTools()`, `pi.setActiveTools()`) is the set of tools declared to the model. `pi.getAllTools()` reports each tool's `exposure`, `namespace`, and `annotations`. `annotations` are hints about what a tool does, with the meaning of MCP tool annotations: `readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, and `openWorldHint`. MCP tools carry the hints their server declares. Missing hints take the MCP defaults: a tool is not read-only, and may be destructive and reach an open world. The hints are not verified, but a permission extension can use them to decide which calls to confirm. This confirms the calls Codex asks approval for: ```typescript pi.on("tool_call", async (event, ctx) => { const hints = pi.getAllTools().find((tool) => tool.name === event.toolName)?.annotations; const needsApproval = hints?.destructiveHint === true || (!hints?.readOnlyHint && ((hints?.destructiveHint ?? true) || (hints?.openWorldHint ?? true))); if (needsApproval && !(await ctx.ui.confirm("Allow tool call?", event.toolName))) { return { block: true, reason: `${event.toolName} was not approved` }; } }); ``` A tool that orchestrates other tools can adjust what the model sees while it is active with `prepareLoadout(loadout)`. It runs whenever the active tools change and receives the declared tools, the callable tools, and every registered tool with its exposure and namespace. It returns replacement `descriptions` for declared tools (including its own) and `hiddenDeclarations`: active tools whose declarations requests leave out while they stay active and callable. `codemode` uses only this hook, `exposure`, and `ctx.executeTool()`, so another tool can implement the same behavior under a different name. ### Activate tools dynamically Register every tool first, keep optional tools inactive, and use `pi.setActiveTools()` from a loader tool to select the desired active tools. Names must already be registered; unknown names are ignored. Pi records the initial prompt and tool set in the transcript's first system message, then appends tool and prompt changes before the next model request. Providers that cannot represent the transition receive a complete transcript checkpoint, which can invalidate the cached prefix. ### Tool rendering A tool's `renderCall` and `renderResult` draw its calls in the interactive transcript and in HTML exports. `pi.registerToolRenderer((toolName, next) => renderers)` chooses renderers for calls to any tool, including tools that are not registered yet, such as MCP tools in a resumed session before their server connected. `next()` returns what the remaining resolvers (in extension load order), then the registered tool, would use, so `next() ?? mine` only fills in. ### MCP servers `pi.registerMcpServer(name, config)` adds an MCP server for the current session. `config` has the shape of an `mcpServers` entry in [`mcp.json`](mcp.md): `command`, `args`, `env`, and `cwd` for stdio servers, `url`, `headers`, and `oauth` for HTTP servers, plus `exposure`, `toolExposure`, `description`, `enabled`, and `timeout`. ```typescript pi.registerMcpServer("jira", { url: "https://mcp.example.com/jira", exposure: "codemode" }); pi.unregisterMcpServer("jira"); ``` Servers registered while the extension loads connect when the session starts, together with the `mcp.json` servers; servers registered later connect right away, and `pi.unregisterMcpServer()` closes the connection and makes the server's tools unreachable. Registrations are not saved: register again on every load, for example based on the extension's own settings. A server in `mcp.json` with the same name takes precedence, and `/mcp` shows the override. Registering the same name again replaces the extension's earlier registration; names registered by another extension, invalid names, and invalid configs throw. The built-in MCP support connects registered servers. When nothing does, because another extension replaced it (see [MCP](mcp.md#other-mcp-extensions)), each registration is reported as an extension error. Other MCP extensions can connect registered servers too: read them with `pi.getMcpServers()` on `session_start` and handle the `mcp_servers_change` event for later changes. ### Context and session changes `ExtensionContext` provides the working directory, mode, UI, session manager, model runtime, abort signal, context usage, and controls for compaction and shutdown. Use `ctx.modelRegistry.streamSimple()` for provider-neutral nested model calls. Command handlers receive `ExtensionCommandContext`, which adds operations for waiting until idle, reloading, tree navigation, and session replacement. These operations are command-only because calling them from lifecycle handlers can deadlock the runtime. Session replacement invalidates the old context. Capture only plain data before switching, then use the fresh context supplied to `withSession` for session-bound work. ### State Choose storage based on how state participates in the conversation: | State | Storage | |---|---| | Tool state that follows the active branch | Tool-result `details` | | Durable data excluded from model context | `pi.appendEntry()` | | Custom content stored and sent to the model | `pi.sendMessage()` | | Data outside one session | External storage | Reconstruct branch-sensitive state from `ctx.sessionManager.getBranch()` during `session_start`. Do not rebuild it from every file entry because abandoned branches represent alternative histories. Register an entry or message renderer when custom stored content should appear in the transcript. ### UI and modes `ctx.ui` provides dialogs, notifications, status text, widgets, titles, editor access, and custom components. Use `ctx.ui.custom()` only when the interaction needs its own rendering and input. See [Terminal UI](tui.md) for component, focus, overlay, theme, and performance guidance. Extensions load in interactive, RPC, JSON, and print modes. Interactive mode provides the complete terminal UI. RPC can forward supported dialogs and notifications through the [RPC Extension UI protocol](rpc-extension-ui.md), but not custom terminal components; JSON and print modes have no UI. Guard terminal-only behavior with `ctx.mode === "tui"` and use `ctx.hasUI` for interactions supported by interactive and RPC clients. Keep tool and event behavior independent from rendering so non-interactive modes remain functional. ### Errors and cleanup Pi reports handler errors and continues where possible. A `tool_call` handler failure blocks the tool as a fail-safe; a tool execution failure becomes an error result for the model. Release resources in `session_shutdown` even when normal operation attempted cleanup. Keep cleanup idempotent because cancellation, reload, session replacement, and process exit can converge on the same path. Use `ctx.shutdown()` to request an orderly process shutdown. ## Examples and reference The checked [extension examples](../examples/extensions/) cover tools, lifecycle events, commands, flags, shortcuts, state, rendering, providers, OAuth, remote execution, and terminal components. Start with the smallest example matching your integration point. Use [Custom Providers](custom-provider.md) for model-service integrations, [Terminal UI](tui.md) for custom components, and [Pi Packages](packages.md) to install or distribute extensions with other resources.

# PRD-010 / #152: integrated research-cycle feasibility

## Scope and evidence

Source: [issue #152](https://github.com/feniix/pi-extensions/issues/152) and
[PRD-010](../prd/PRD-010-pi-exa-integrated-research-cycle.md).
This is feasibility/design work, not the integrated-cycle implementation.
No live Exa calls were made. One operator-requested TypeSafe design-selection
request used Jev; it is not a proposed runtime dependency.

Verified baseline: committed lockfile, pnpm 12.8.1, `exa-js` 2.23.0,
Pi 1.0.3, bridgekit 0.15.0. The initial local Pi installation was 0.86.1;
`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` restored the graph without changing dependencies.
Distinguish documented remote capabilities, observed installed/offline behavior,
proposed contracts, and unverified runtime/account guarantees.

## Agent capability matrix

| Capability | Evidence and limits |
|---|---|
| Structured output | Documented `outputSchema` / `output.structured`; SDK forwards schema and retains data. SDK typing does not validate schemas or prove evidence. |
| Grounding | Documented optional field-level citations; SDK preserves them. Local formatter flattens citations; future envelope must retain associations. |
| Input records | `input.data` means processing/enrichment rows, not evidence attachments. `input.exclusion` excludes returned entities, not reading or security filtering. |
| Selected evidence | No dedicated source-pack field established. Use labeled query context, not processing rows. Source fidelity remains unverified. |
| Continuation | Completed same-team `previousRunId` creates a new run; not polling, recovery, or idempotency. ZDR cannot assume continuation support. |
----

# PRD-010 / #171: Pi host capabilities for guided background research

Research date: 2026-10-12 UTC. Target host: Pi 1.1.0 (`@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`,
the latest 1.x at the time; the workspace pin moved from 1.0.3 in this slice).
Exa SDK: `exa-js` 2.23.0 (unchanged). Source: issue #171, PRD-010 v1.3 and the
[architecture contract](../architecture/plan-pi-exa-integrated-research-cycle.md).

## Scope and evidence boundary

This document records what the pinned Pi host can and cannot guarantee for the
6.1.0 journey: request → clarify → preview scope/cost → trusted approval →
submit → return the research ID and control → background monitoring →
completion notification → report. Evidence comes from three sources, each
labeled below:

- **Docs**: the shipped `docs/*.md` and `dist/**/*.d.ts` of Pi 1.1.0.
- **Source**: the shipped `dist/core/agent-session.js`, `dist/core/extensions/runner.js`
  and `dist/modes/rpc/rpc-mode.js` of Pi 1.1.0 (line references are to that build).
- **Experiment**: the runnable prototype in
  `packages/pi-exa/__tests__/fixtures/guided-prototype/` driven by
  `packages/pi-exa/__tests__/guided-prototype.test.ts` (in-process SDK session,
  scripted model) and `packages/pi-exa/__tests__/guided-prototype.rpc.test.ts`
  (a real `pi --mode rpc` child process). Both use a controllable mocked Exa job.

No paid Exa call, live model call, interactive TUI smoke or publication was
performed. The prototype is design evidence; it does not implement PRD-010 and
does not touch the merged v1.2 foundation. An interactive TUI demonstration is the
#175 gate.

## Capability matrix

| Requirement | Pi 1.1.0 capability | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trusted operator approval in the normal guided flow | `ctx.ui.confirm(title, message, { timeout, signal })` is available to tool `execute()` through `ExtensionToolContext`; it blocks the tool until the dialog resolves. Only extension code that received a `true` result can write a grant; no tool parameter can carry one. | Docs `extensions/types.d.ts` (`ExtensionUIContext.confirm`, `ExtensionUIDialogOptions`); Experiment: SDK test "approves through the trusted dialog" and RPC test (dialog title/body carried the proposal, `timeout: 600000`). | Supported |
| Confirmation in RPC/headless clients | RPC forwards `confirm` as `extension_ui_request` and resolves `false` on `cancelled: true` or timeout; `ctx.hasUI` is `true` in TUI and RPC. Print/JSON modes bind no UI: `hasUI` is `false` and the default `confirm` resolves `false`. | Source `runner.js` (`noOpUIContext.confirm: async () => false`; `hasUI()` is `uiContext !== noOpUIContext`), `rpc-mode.js:85`; Docs `rpc-extension-ui.md`; Experiment: SDK test "fails closed without a trusted confirmation surface" (`hasUI=false`, `APPROVAL_UNAVAILABLE`, zero creates), RPC test cancelled dialog → `APPROVAL_NOT_GRANTED`. | Supported; fail closed on `hasUI === false` before calling `confirm`, because a silent `false` is indistinguishable from a decline |
| Distinguish decline, dismissal and timeout | `confirm` returns a bare boolean. The extension cannot tell a decline from a timeout or a cancelled dialog. | Docs `ExtensionUIContext.confirm(): Promise<boolean>`. | Unsupported; report "not granted" and never infer consent |
| Tool returns while the remote job is pending | A tool `execute()` may return after the create acknowledgement; later work continues on extension-owned timers. `pi.sendMessage` is usable from a timer callback (no `ctx` needed). | Experiment: SDK and RPC tests show the tool result "Research started: run_1 … status running" while the mock job stays `running`, followed by an intervening user prompt. | Supported |
| Background scheduling while Pi runs | Node timers started from a tool or `session_start` and cleared in `session_shutdown`. Pi forbids starting timers in the extension factory. | Docs `extensions.md` "Respect the runtime lifecycle"; Experiment: monitor timers in the prototype. | Supported (in-process only; nothing runs after Pi exits) |
| Safe-turn assistant wakeup | `pi.sendMessage(message, { triggerTurn: true, deliverAs: "followUp" })`: idle → appends the custom message and starts a turn now; streaming → queues it after pending work; during `agent_settled` emission → deferred until settlement completes. `deliverAs: "steer"` would enter after the current assistant turn instead. | Source `agent-session.js` `sendCustomMessage` (lines ~1770–1800, `_isEmittingAgentSettled`, `_deferredSettledActions`); Experiment: SDK test "queues a completion that lands during an active response" shows the notice appended after the streaming assistant message, then the report turn. | Supported |
| Safe boundary signal for extensions | `agent_settled` (now with `aborted`) is the final notification-only boundary; `agent_before_settle` and `turn_end` are actionable. `ctx.isIdle()` and `ctx.hasPendingMessages()` exist but timers have no `ctx`; relying on Pi's queue is sufficient. | Docs `extensions.md`; Pi 1.1.0 changelog (`aborted` on `agent_settled`); Experiment: `agent_settled:aborted=true` observed after `session.abort()`. | Supported |
| Delivery acknowledgement | `pi.sendMessage` returns `void`; rejections are reported as extension errors, not to the caller. There is no API-level acknowledgement. Pi appends a `custom_message` entry to the session file when it actually delivers; an extension can observe that entry (with its own `details`) through `ctx.sessionManager.getEntries()` on `agent_settled` or `session_start`. | Source `agent-session.js` `runner.bindCore({ sendMessage: … .catch(emitError) })`, `_appendCustomMessage`; Docs `session-format.md` (`custom_message` entries); Experiment: `notice_acknowledged` after locating the entry; RPC `get_entries` shows `custom_message:exa-proto-completion`. | Partially supported: acknowledgement by observation, not by return value |
| Durability of queued deliveries | Streaming-time queues (`steer`, `followUp`, `nextTurn`, deferred custom messages) live in process memory until Pi appends them. A crash between `sendMessage` and the append loses the host copy; only the extension's own pending record survives. | Source `agent-session.js` `_pendingCustomMessages`, `_pendingNextTurnMessages`, `agent.followUp/steer`. | Unsupported exactly-once; keep a durable pending notice and reconcile |
| Origin-session targeting | One extension runtime serves one session. `ctx.sessionManager.getSessionId()` identifies it at `session_start`. There is no API to deliver into another session. Session replacement (new/resume/fork/switch) emits `session_shutdown` and invalidates the old runtime; later use of the old `pi` throws the stale-context error. SDK `session.dispose()` invalidates without emitting `session_shutdown`. | Source `agent-session.js` `dispose()` → `runner.invalidate(...)`, `runner.js` `invalidate`; Experiment: SDK test "fences delivery after the runtime is invalidated" (`notice_delivery_failed`, `deliveryError` contains "stale", a second session with a different ID discovers but does not deliver the foreign notice); RPC test `new_session` → monitor `paused:SHUTDOWN`. | Supported for same-session delivery; cross-session delivery unsupported by design |
| Discoverability after restart | `session_start` carries `reason: startup | reload | new | resume | fork` and a `ctx` with the session ID; durable state outside the session must be read by the extension. Nothing resumes implicitly. | Docs `SessionStartEvent`; Experiment: pending notices reported with origin/foreign classification; previous runtime monitors marked `paused:RESTART`. | Supported |
| Blocked-on-dialog visibility | Pi 1.1.0 reports `blocked` with the dialog title through OSC 7501 to supporting terminals and emits `ui_prompt_start/end` extension events. | Docs `terminal-setup.md` "Program status"; `extensions/types.d.ts` `UIPromptStartEvent`. | Supported (informational) |
| Server retry guidance for GET backoff | `ExaError` exposes `statusCode`, `type`, `code`, `detail`; no `Retry-After` value is surfaced by the pinned SDK. | Docs `exa-js` `dist/index.d.ts` `class ExaError`. | Unsupported; use local backoff |
| Create abort / server idempotency | Not assumed. The prototype never cancels and the SDK create is not aborted; an unacknowledged create stays `unknown` and a late acknowledgement settles the original attempt. | Experiment: SDK test "keeps an unacknowledged create unknown and saves a genuine late run ID without resubmitting" (`late_ack`, one create). | Unsupported by design; fail closed |

## Experiment summary

The SDK test (`guided-prototype.test.ts`) proves, against a real Pi 1.1.0
`AgentSession` with a scripted `pi-ai` faux model and no network:

1. Trusted approval, one mocked create, the saved run ID returned while the job is
   pending, an intervening user turn, one completion notice delivered at a settled
   boundary and acknowledged by its `custom_message` entry; terminal facts were
   persisted before the notice was scheduled.
2. Headless (`hasUI=false`): `APPROVAL_UNAVAILABLE`, zero creates.
3. Declined dialog: `APPROVAL_NOT_GRANTED`, zero creates, proposal still open.
4. Superseded proposal: `PROPOSAL_STALE`, no dialog, zero creates.
5. Completion during an active response: notice appended after the streaming
   answer, then a report turn; repeated terminal observations yield one notice.
6. Aborting the chat turn: `agent_settled aborted=true`, no remote cancel, job
   still running, completion delivered later, still one create.
7. Transient GET errors back off with growing delays; exhausted errors pause with
   `TRANSIENT_EXHAUSTED` while the remote status stays `running` and no outcome or
   notice is fabricated; timers are released.
8. `401` → `AUTH` pause; lost run (`404`) → `NOT_FOUND` pause; no cancel.
9. Unacknowledged create → `SUBMISSION_UNKNOWN` with no run ID; the late genuine
   ID is saved on the original attempt with monitoring `LATE_ACKNOWLEDGEMENT`
   paused; still one create.
10. Disposed runtime: delivery throws the stale-context error, the notice stays
    pending with the error recorded; a different session discovers the foreign
    notice and does not deliver it.

The RPC test (`guided-prototype.rpc.test.ts`) repeats the happy path in a real
`pi --mode rpc` process: the client answers the forwarded `confirm`
(`timeout: 600000`), prompts while the job is pending, completes the job through
`/exa-proto complete run_1` (disposition `handled`), observes the appended
`custom_message` and report through `get_entries`, replaces the session with
`new_session` (second attempt's monitor → `paused:SHUTDOWN`), and sends
`cancelled: true` for a third dialog (`APPROVAL_NOT_GRANTED`, zero creates in the
replaced runtime).

Run the prototype interactively with your own model:

```bash
pi -e packages/pi-exa/__tests__/fixtures/guided-prototype/pi-entry.ts
# ask for research, approve the dialog, then: /exa-proto complete run_1
```

## Unsupported guarantees (explicit)

- No exactly-once completion notification across crashes. The host offers no
  delivery acknowledgement API and holds queued deliveries in memory.
- No delivery into a session other than the one the runtime serves. Detached
  origins keep pending notices for explicit resume.
- No notifications after Pi exits. Monitoring is an in-process feature.
- No distinction between decline, dismissal and timeout of the approval dialog.
- No server retry guidance, create abort or idempotency from the Exa SDK.
- No evidence about interactive TUI rendering of the dialog or notice; that is
  the #175 interactive smoke.

## Consequences for the implementation contract

The settled public actions, consent binding, time bounds, cadence/backoff and
pause limits derived from this evidence are recorded in the architecture plan
section "#171 settled implementation contract". The qualification map carries a
#171 evidence row pointing at the two experiments.

  observation coordination so it cannot overlap a running check.

### Consent binding

`proposalId = hash(artifactHash, revision, assessmentBasis)`. The dialog body is the
rendered proposal; the operator never copies the hash. A plan edit changes the
artifact hash and therefore supersedes the proposal: approval of a superseded or
consumed proposal fails with `PROPOSAL_STALE` before any dialog or create. Decline,
dismissal, timeout and headless invocation are indistinguishable "not granted"
results; none is a consent event and none consumes the proposal.

### Submission and observation bounds

| Bound | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Create acknowledgement wait | 30 s | Separates acknowledgement from the 180 s full-run default; Exa creates return an ID in seconds. Expiry leaves the attempt `unknown`; a genuine late ID settles the original attempt with monitoring paused (`LATE_ACKNOWLEDGEMENT`). |
| Per-GET deadline | 15 s | One bounded request; deadlines never hold storage locks. |
| First check after acknowledgement | 5 s | Agent runs rarely finish sooner; avoids an immediate wasted GET. |
| Backoff | ×1.5 per pending observation or transient failure, capped at 60 s, ±20 % jitter, non-overlapping (the next check is scheduled only after the previous one completes) | Keeps long runs cheap while bounding notification latency to about one minute. |
| Transient failures | pause after 8 consecutive failures or 10 min without a successful GET | `ExaError` exposes no retry guidance, so local limits apply. |
| Auth (401/403) and not-found (404) | pause immediately (`AUTH`, `NOT_FOUND`) | Not proof of remote failure; remote outcome and liability stay separate. |
| Monitor lifetime | pause after 3 h (`MONITOR_LIFETIME`) | Exa publishes no maximum duration; explicit resume restarts observation without create. |
| Approval dialog timeout | 10 min | Expiry grants nothing. |

Monitoring has no create, continuation, retry, replacement or cancel authority.
Interrupting a chat turn aborts only the model turn: the saved run and its
liability continue; no cancel request is issued.

### Completion delivery protocol

1. On a terminal observation persist remote status, stop reason, classified usage
   and the local processing outcome on the attempt.
2. Persist one notice per attempt/terminal outcome with state `pending`. Repeated
   terminal observations of the same attempt create no second notice.
3. Deliver with `pi.sendMessage({ customType: "exa-research-completion", content:
   <attempt reference and read-only instruction>, display: true, details:
   { noticeId, cycleId, attemptId, runId, status } }, { triggerTurn: true,
   deliverAs: "followUp" })`. Idle origin → wakes now; streaming origin → after
   pending work; never `steer`. Content is a reference, never vendor output.
   Mark the notice `sent`.
4. Acknowledge by observation: on `agent_settled` or `session_start`, find the
   `custom_message` entry carrying `details.noticeId` in the session and mark the
   notice `acknowledged` with the entry ID. A `sent` notice without an entry after
   restart is `uncertain` and is reconciled, not re-sent automatically and not
   dropped. Exactly-once is not claimed.
5. A stale runtime (session replacement, reload, SDK dispose) throws on
   `sendMessage`; keep the notice `pending`, record the error, and let the origin
   session's `session_start` discovery surface it. Foreign sessions report but
   never deliver another session's notice.

### Lifecycle fences

Stop timers and mark monitors `paused:SHUTDOWN` on `session_shutdown` for every
reason; `session_start` marks any monitor left `registered`/`running` as
`paused:RESTART` and reports pending notices without delivering them. Explicit
resume (#174) reacquires ownership and restarts eligible monitors. Archive stops
monitoring and delivery and warns that remote work may continue.

### State dimensions

Keep four independent dimensions on each attempt: local submission
(`submitting`/`acknowledged`/`unknown`), remote lifecycle (`queued`/`running`/
`completed`/`failed`/`cancelled` plus stop reason), monitoring (`none`/
`registered`/`running`/`paused:<reason>`/`stopped`) and delivery
(`pending`/`sent`/`acknowledged`/`uncertain`). A paused monitor is not a failed
run; a sent notice is not a delivered one.

- `feat(pi-exa)`: persist host-owned monitor and completion-notice records. New `research-monitor.ts` with the settled bounds, the versioned monitor/notice schema, error classification, backoff/pause policy and notice text. The cycle record gains an optional `monitors` array; `registerMonitor` records intent in the owning session, `updateMonitor` applies operation-bound facts without acquiring ownership.
- `feat(pi-exa)`: monitor approved research in the background and deliver completion. Registration after acknowledgement returns control promptly (registration failure still returns the saved run ID with `monitoring: "paused"`). Bounded, non-overlapping same-run GETs through the existing recovery capability (first after 5 s, ×1.5 backoff to 60 s with jitter; pause after 8 transient failures or 10 min silence, immediately on auth/not-found, after 3 h). No create, retry, replace or cancel authority. Terminal facts, classified usage and local validation are persisted by the lifecycle observer before one notice per attempt is recorded and delivered with `pi.sendMessage({ triggerTurn: true, deliverAs: "followUp" })`; `agent_settled` acknowledges it by observing the persisted `exa-research-completion` entry. Shutdown/switch/fork/tree/archive pause monitors; session start pauses stale monitors, marks sent-but-unconfirmed notices `uncertain` and surfaces pending notices without delivering them elsewhere. Explicit recover and the monitor share observation coordination. New `--exa-monitor-interval-ms` flag.
- `fix(pi-exa)`: storage errors in the tick pause the monitor (`STORAGE`) instead of escaping as unhandled rejections; the detach latch lifts on live registration so tree navigation does not leave a dead "registered" monitor.
- `docs(pi-exa)`: README monitoring/completion/fence sections, planner skill guidance, changelog.

## Capability note for reviewers

The cycle registration is installed inside Pi's own `session_start` dispatch (flags resolve after factories load), so its `session_start` handler never fires for the first session. The registration now exposes `sessionStarted(ctx)` and the entry point invokes it explicitly; later starts use the handler.

## Tests

`guided-monitoring.test.ts` (registered extension, real private filesystem controller, mocked Exa SDK, host simulated at the `pi.sendMessage`/`getEntries` boundary): normal wakeup and acknowledgement with bounded GETs and one notice; registration failure after create; transient backoff then `TRANSIENT_EXHAUSTED`, `AUTH`, `NOT_FOUND` pauses with the remote status still `running`; failed and local-invalid completions with recovery guidance; shutdown/restart/archive fences; storage failure after a GET and tree-navigation recovery; uncertain notice on restart; two isolated sessions. Zero cancels, one create per approval throughout.

Run: `pnpm run check`, `pnpm run test` (1053 passed), `pnpm exec vitest run --coverage packages/pi-exa/__tests__`, `node scripts/check-release-changelog.mjs packages/pi-exa`.

## Honest limits

- Safe-boundary delivery during an active response relies on Pi's queue and is proven by the #171 SDK and RPC experiments; the registered-host harness cannot stream.
- No interactive TUI run (#175). No cross-session delivery by design; detached origins keep pending notices for explicit resume (#174 completes restart/competing-runtime recovery).

## Decision requested

`researchMode=active` remains the foundation's blocking path for already opted-in callers; guided requests route to `submit`. Unchanged from #176/#177.

Closes #173.
