cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-feniix-src-personal-pi-pi-extensions/90caff9b-07c1-45ca-be6f-308aff547939/scratchpad/pr-recovery.md <<'EOF'
## Summary

Fourth layer of the pi-exa 6.1.0 stack (#174, stacked on #179): background research survives local interruptions without duplicate remote work or lost outcomes. Restart discovers saved runs and pending notices; an explicit conversational resume picks them up.

**Package:** `@feniix/pi-exa` (opted-in Pi cycle path only; standalone, default-opt-out and MCP behavior unchanged).

## Changes

- `feat(pi-exa)`: recover monitoring and notifications across interruptions.
  - Explicit resume (`exa_research_status action=resume` or `/exa-research resume`) reacquires ownership, re-registers eligible paused monitors for the existing saved run (no create, no reservation), creates the notice missing for a terminal attempt whose scheduling crashed, and delivers pending or uncertain notices into the resuming session. Re-sent notices are labeled possible duplicates of the same single run; exactly-once is not claimed. Resume iterates saved attempts, so runs whose monitor registration failed after the create are recovered too.
  - Start discovery pauses only monitors whose cycle owner is absent or proven dead (`ESRCH`); a live owner elsewhere keeps observing and competing resumes are refused. Age alone never authorizes takeover.
  - A tick whose GET was in flight when the monitor was paused, archived or detached keeps the late original facts but schedules no notice for the detached context. Repeated resume never duplicates ticks; a detach latch lifts on a successful resume so delivery is reported honestly (`notice delivered` / `notice re-sent` / `notice pending`).
- `docs(pi-exa)`: README recovery section, planner skill guidance, changelog.

## Tests

`guided-recovery.test.ts` (registered extension, real private filesystem store, mocked Exa SDK; restart simulated by `session_shutdown` plus a fresh runtime over the same store): shutdown preservation and discovery without ownership or GETs; conversational resume with one delivery and one create; competing live runtime refused with no duplicate monitor; notice-scheduling crash recovered on resume; uncertain notice re-sent as a possible duplicate; late facts after archive without reactivation; duplicate-tick guard and tree navigation then resume; registration-failure run resumed; remote-ID publication crash kept unknown (`RECOVERY_UNAVAILABLE` names the missing ID, submission blocked); proven-dead owner paused on start and resumed by the next session; local-invalid result revalidated within the frozen contract with no consent inferred.

Run: `pnpm run check`, `pnpm run test`, `pnpm exec vitest run --coverage packages/pi-exa/__tests__`, `node scripts/check-release-changelog.mjs packages/pi-exa`.

## Honest limits

- Crash points are filesystem fault injection in one process, not separate-process or power-loss reproduction (as the qualification document already states).
- Live-owner refusal is proven in-process with a shared pid; dead-owner recovery via a written dead pid.
- Local interruption keeps an attempt `unknown` while its saved run ID, frozen artifact, grants and liability survive; the remote run is never declared failed locally.
- No interactive TUI run (#175).

## Decision requested

`researchMode=active` remains the foundation's blocking path for already opted-in callers; guided requests route to `submit`. Unchanged from #176–#179.

Closes #174.
EOF

Host-owned observation of one acknowledged Agent run while Pi is open: bounded,
non-overlapping GETs with backoff, persisted as a monitor record on the cycle
(state, pause reason, counters). It has no create, retry, replace or cancel
authority; a paused monitor is not a failed run, and the remote work and its
liability continue regardless.

*Avoid:* polling loop in the assistant, or remote cancellation.

The one durable record per attempt and terminal outcome that schedules the
originating session's wakeup (`exa-research-completion` custom message). Its state
is `pending`, `sent`, `acknowledged` (the persisted session entry was observed) or

possible duplicate; exactly-once delivery across crashes is not claimed.

Done. The whole #171 to #175 stack is implemented, pushed, and green in CI at every PR's current head.

**Pull requests, bottom to top, all ready for review and passing CI**
- #176 prototype and settled host contract: https://github.com/feniix/pi-extensions/pull/176
- #177 guided submission through approved dialog: https://github.com/feniix/pi-extensions/pull/177
- #179 background monitoring and completion delivery: https://github.com/feniix/pi-extensions/pull/179
- #180 recovery across interruptions: https://github.com/feniix/pi-extensions/pull/180
- #181 offline qualification of the complete journey: https://github.com/feniix/pi-extensions/pull/181

**What the stack delivers**
- A user says "research Laya versus Jev". The assistant starts a non-spending cycle, records the brief, renders a readable scope and cost proposal, and submits only after Pi's own confirmation dialog says yes. One create, run ID returned while the job is still pending.
- A host-owned monitor polls that saved run with bounded backoff while the user keeps chatting. Terminal facts persist first, then one completion notice wakes the originating session, acknowledged by observing the persisted session entry. Monitoring has no create, retry, replace or cancel authority.
- Shutdown, restart, archive, tree navigation and competing runtimes are fenced. Explicit resume reacquires ownership, re-registers paused monitors and reconciles pending or uncertain notices without claiming exactly-once.
- Two pre-existing bugs fixed along the way: Pi registers flags by bare name and applies values after factories run, so the documented `--exa-*` options did not parse on Pi 1.x before this stack. They do now, and tool enablement refreshes at `session_start`.

**Gates passed locally and in CI:** frozen install, lint, typecheck, 1067 tests, pi-exa coverage at 93% lines and 86% branches, MCP build, changelog check, dependency audit.

**Honest limits**
- The production smoke drives a real `pi --mode rpc` process with real `exa-js` against a mock HTTP server. It proves the host protocol, not terminal rendering.
- Crash points are in-process filesystem fault injection, not separate-process or power-loss reproduction.
- No cross-session delivery by design. Zero paid Exa or model calls were made.

**Decisions that are yours**
1. `researchMode=active` is kept as the foundation's blocking path while guided requests route to `submit`. You have not said whether to hide it behind `submit` instead; the plan flags this as pending.
2. Merge bottom-up with `gh stack merge <pr> --yes`, starting at #176.
3. The 6.1.0 version and date bump is still in your stash, untouched. Release, tag and publish need your separate go-ahead.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/feniix/.claude/skills/herdr

# Herdr

Herdr is a terminal multiplexer and runtime for coding agents. It organizes terminals into workspaces, tabs, and panes, detects agent identity and status, and exposes the running session through the `herdr` CLI.

Before issuing any control command, check that this agent is running inside a Herdr-managed pane:

```bash
test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1
```

If the check fails, say that you are not running inside Herdr and stop. Do not inspect or control the focused Herdr session from outside Herdr.

When the check passes, the `herdr` binary in `PATH` talks to the running session. Use it to inspect neighboring work, create isolated terminal contexts, start agents and commands, read their output, and wait for state changes.

## Learn the current CLI

The installed binary is the authority for command syntax. Begin with:

```bash
herdr --help
```

Then print the relevant command group by running it without a subcommand:

```bash
herdr pane
herdr workspace
herdr worktree
herdr tab
herdr wait
herdr terminal
herdr notification
herdr integration
herdr session
```

Do not run bare `herdr` for discovery; it launches or attaches the TUI. Do not probe a mutating nested command by omitting arguments; some commands, including `herdr workspace create`, are valid with defaults and will execute. Use the command-group output above instead.

Most control commands print JSON. Read identifiers and state from those responses instead of predicting either one.

## IDs and current context

Public IDs are short stable handles:

- workspace: `w1`
- tab: `w1:t1`
- pane: `w1:p1`
- terminal: `term_...`

The encoded suffix can contain letters and can grow beyond one character. Treat every ID as an opaque string.

Closed tab and pane IDs are not reused and do not retarget later resources. A pane moved into another workspace receives a new public pane ID. Re-read create, split, move, list, or get responses after mutations; never construct an ID from a workspace or display number.

Herdr injects the caller's stable context into every managed pane:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID" "$HERDR_TAB_ID" "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Prefer `--current` when a pane command should target the calling pane. Omitting a target can use the UI-focused pane, which may belong to the user or another client.

Discover live state with:

```bash
herdr workspace list
herdr tab list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr pane current --current
herdr pane list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
```

## Control agents through panes

An agent runs inside a pane. Use the pane ID as the control target for agents, shells, servers, tests, and logs. This keeps spawning, input, reads, waits, and cleanup on one stable control surface.

Use workspace and tab commands for organization. Use worktree commands only when you intentionally want Herdr to create, open, or remove a Git checkout.

Pane records expose `agent`, `agent_status`, and native session metadata when available. Agent status is `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, or `unknown`.

`idle` and `done` are the same underlying semantic state with different attention state:

- `idle`: the agent is waiting and its result is considered seen.
- `done`: the agent finished and its result has not been seen.

An agent that first opens at its prompt reports `idle`, including in a background pane. After a working or blocked agent completes, it reports `done` when its tab or workspace is in the background. It reports `idle` when it completes in the active tab while the foreground client is focused. If the foreground client is explicitly unfocused, completion can become `done` even in the active tab.

Focusing a pane, switching to its tab, or regaining outer terminal focus marks the visible tab as seen, so `done` becomes `idle`. Switching away does not turn an existing `idle` status into `done`; `done` is created by a later completion while the pane is unseen. With no foreground client, a new completion in the globally active tab is treated as seen while completions in background tabs still become `done`.

## Start agents interactively

Default to a sibling pane in the current tab and current working directory. Do not create a workspace, tab, worktree, or different cwd unless the user explicitly requests that topology or location.

Honor a direction requested by the user. Otherwise inspect the caller pane's current rectangle:

```bash
herdr pane layout --pane "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Split a wide pane to the right and a narrow or tall pane down. Avoid repeated same-direction splits that would create unusably narrow columns or short rows. Keep the user's focus in the calling pane:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --no-focus
```

Replace `right` with `down` when the layout calls for it.

Read `result.pane.pane_id` from the JSON response. Give the pane a useful label, then start the requested agent by running only its normal executable so its interactive TUI opens:

```bash
herdr pane rename <returned-pane-id> "reviewer"
herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "codex"
```

Use the executable that belongs to the requested agent:

- Codex: `codex`
- Claude Code: `claude`
- pi: `pi`
- OpenCode: `opencode`
- OMP: `omp`

Do not pass the task as an argv prompt by default. Do not add non-interactive flags. Only change the normal interactive launch when the user explicitly asks for a different launch mode or command.

Inspect the pane after launch. If `agent_status` is not yet `idle`, wait for the idle transition. Once it is idle, submit the task with `pane run`:

```bash
herdr pane get <returned-pane-id>
herdr wait agent-status <returned-pane-id> --status idle --timeout 30000
herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "Review the current diff and report only actionable findings."
```

Status waits match the current status immediately or wait for a future matching transition.

`pane run` sends the text and Enter together. Use it for initial prompts and follow-ups instead of coordinating `send-text` and `send-keys` separately.

For normal background work, wait for the agent to start working. If the pane remains in a background tab or workspace, wait for `done` before reading its transcript:

```bash
herdr wait agent-status <returned-pane-id> --status working --timeout 30000
herdr wait agent-status <returned-pane-id> --status done --timeout 120000
herdr pane read <returned-pane-id> --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

If the user is watching that tab, completion reports `idle` instead, so wait for `idle`. Always treat either `idle` or `done` as completed when inspecting `pane get`; the difference is whether the result has been seen.

If a wait times out, inspect `herdr pane get <returned-pane-id>` and `pane read` before deciding what to do. A `blocked` agent needs input; an `unknown` pane may not yet contain a detected or integrated agent.

Submit follow-ups the same way:

```bash
herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "Now check the failing test."
```

## Run an ordinary command in another pane

Split the calling pane using the same geometry rule without moving the user's focus:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --no-focus
```

Read the new `pane_id` from the JSON response, then run and inspect the command:

```bash
herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "just test"
herdr wait output <returned-pane-id> --match "test result" --timeout 120000
herdr pane read <returned-pane-id> --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

Inspect existing output before waiting for future output. A wait timeout exits with status `1`.

Use the read source that matches the task:

- `visible`: the current rendered viewport
- `recent`: recent scrollback as rendered, including soft wraps
- `recent-unwrapped`: recent scrollback with soft wraps joined; prefer it for logs and transcripts
- `detection`: the bottom-buffer snapshot used by agent detection

Use `--format ansi` when colors and terminal styling are evidence. Otherwise use text.

If the user explicitly asks for another tab, workspace, or worktree, discover that command group and use returned IDs. Do not infer a larger topology from a request to start an agent or command.

## Safety and coordination rules

- Use `--no-focus` for background work unless the user asked to switch context.
- Use `--current` or an explicit ID. Do not rely on another client's focused pane.
- Parse IDs from JSON responses. Do not derive them from sidebar order or examples.
- Inspect before waiting. Read current output first, then wait for the next state or output you expect.
- Do not close workspaces, tabs, panes, or sessions you did not create unless the user explicitly asked.
- Never run `herdr server stop` from an active session unless the user explicitly intends to stop the server and its pane processes.
- Never kill the main Herdr process. Use named test sessions for experiments that need an isolated server.

# i-have-adhd

The reader has ADHD. Output is not just brief. It is shaped so an ADHD brain can act on it.

## Persistence

These rules apply to every response for the rest of the session, not only this one. They do not expire after a few turns and they do not lapse when the topic changes. If you are unsure whether they still apply, they do.

Turn them off only when the reader says "stop adhd mode" or "normal mode". Confirm in one line, then return to your default style.

## What ADHD changes about reading

Five facts drive every rule below:

1. Working memory is small. Anything not on screen is forgotten. Do not ask the reader to "keep in mind X."
2. Knowing the answer is not doing the answer. The friction between "got it" and "done it" is where work dies.
3. Starting is the hardest step. The first action must be obvious, small, and doable now.
4. Time estimates feel uniform. "A bit of work" and "a few hours" register the same. Vague estimates fail.
5. Dopamine is scarce. Visible progress matters. Buried wins do not register.

## Rules

### 1. Lead with the next action

The first line is something the reader can do. Not context. Not a plan. The action.

Bad: "Let's think about this. Your auth flow has a few moving pieces..."
Good: "Run `npm install jsonwebtoken`, then edit `src/auth.ts:42`."

If the answer is a command, path, or snippet, it goes first. Prose comes after, if at all.

### 2. Number multi-step tasks

If the work takes more than one step, write a numbered list. Each step is one bounded action. No step contains "and then" twice.

Use the fewest steps that still work. Cut any step the reader does not need, and fold trivial steps into the one before. A short path finished beats a complete path abandoned.

Bad: "First open the file, find the function, swap it out, then run the tests."

Good:
```
1. Open `src/auth.ts`
2. Replace `verifyToken` (lines 42 to 58) with the snippet below
3. Run `npm test -- auth.spec.ts`
```

### 3. End with one concrete next action

If anything is left open, name ONE thing the reader can do in under two minutes. Even "open the file" counts.

Bad: "Hope that helps. Let me know if you want to dig deeper."
Good: "Next: run `npm test` and paste the first failing line."

### 4. Suppress tangents

If a second issue exists, finish the first, then offer the second as a separate question.

Bad: "Here's the fix. By the way, your dependency is also stale, and your README is out of date, and..."
Good: "Here's the fix. Separately: there is also a stale dependency. Want me to handle that next?"

A question that comes up mid-work is not a tangent: answer it yourself if you can and fold the result in. If it still needs the reader, surface it once, at the end.

### 5. Restate state every turn

The reader cannot hold "we are on step 3 of 5" between messages. Restate it.

Bad: "Done. Ready for the next part?"
Good: "Step 3 of 5 done: schema updated. Next: backfill the new column. Run the script?"

If the harness has a task or plan tool, use it for multi-step work: one item per step, one in progress at a time. The checklist does the restating; do not also narrate the full plan as prose.

### 6. Give specific time estimates

Vague estimates fail. Ballpark in concrete units.

Bad: "This will take some work."
Good: "About 15 minutes if tests already cover this. An afternoon if not."

### 7. Make completed work visible

Show what now works, in concrete terms. Do not bury wins in a recap.

Bad: "I've made some changes to the auth flow. Among other things..."
Good: "Login now works with magic links. Try: `npm run dev`, open `/login`."

### 8. Matter-of-fact tone for errors

Never use "Uh oh," "Oh no," or "There seems to be a problem." State cause and fix.

Bad: "Uh oh, the test is failing. There seems to be an issue..."
Good: "Test fails at `auth.spec.ts:42`: expected 200, got 401. Cause: missing auth header. Fix: add `Authorization: Bearer ${token}` to the request."

### 9. Cap lists to 5 items

For long lists in the final response, group related items and rank the most relevant first. Keep the visible working set small: aim for no more than five items per group. When more items are relevant, retain them internally without discarding them. Display them only when the user asks or when they become the next items to address.

Never omit relevant items when completeness matters. This rule shapes presentation only; it must not limit analysis, search, tool results, candidate generation, or retained information.

### 10. No preamble, no recap, no closing pleasantries

Forbidden openers: "Great question," "Let me...", "I'll...", "Sure!", "Looking at your...", "To answer your question..."

Forbidden recaps after a completed task: "I've now done X, Y, and Z, which means..."

Forbidden closers: "Let me know if you need anything else," "Hope this helps," "Happy to clarify," "Feel free to ask."

Start with the answer. End when the answer is done.

## When to break the rules

Override the defaults when:

1. User asks to "explain" or "walk me through." Explain fully. Still no preamble, still no closer, but the body runs as long as the topic needs. Add headers so the reader can skim back.
2. Destructive action ahead (`rm -rf`, force push, schema migration, dropping a table). Confirm before acting. Safety wins over brevity.
3. Debug spiral. If the last three turns have been "still broken," stop iterating on code. Name the assumption that might be wrong. Ask one diagnostic question.
4. Real ambiguity in the request. One short clarifying question beats guessing and rewriting.
5. A rule fights the task. When a rule would delete the answer itself, the task wins; the shape stays. Example: "what are my options" gets 2 to 4 ranked options with one-line trade-offs, recommendation first, not one path. The options are the answer.
6. A rule fights the harness. Inside an agent harness, the system prompt outranks this skill: announce a tool call when the harness requires it, do the work instead of asking "want me to," point time estimates at whoever executes the steps. Same principle as 5: the constraint wins, the shape stays.

## Pre-send check

Before sending, delete:

1. The first sentence if it announces what you are about to do.
2. The last sentence if it asks "anything else?" or recaps what just happened.
3. Any "by the way" sidebar.
4. Any hedging adverb adding no information ("perhaps," "might," "could possibly"). Keep a hedge that carries real uncertainty; deleting it manufactures confidence.
5. Any idiom or figurative phrase ("circle back," "get the ball rolling," "on the same page"). Replace with the literal action.

Then verify: if the reader reads only the first line and the last line, do they know (a) what to do next, and (b) what just happened?

If yes, send.

what does researchMode=active do?

`active` is the old blocking way to run a cycle's Agent research. It submits the compiled request and then waits inside the tool call, polling until the run finishes, and cancels the remote run if you interrupt or the 180 s timeout hits.

How it differs from the new `submit`:

| | `active` (old) | `submit` (new, guided) |
|---|---|---|
| Approval | Operator types two slash commands first: `/exa-research approve` and `/exa-research approve-request <hash>` | Pi dialog, no commands or hashes |
| Behavior | Blocks the conversation until the run ends | Returns the run ID immediately, monitors in background |
| Interrupt | Cancels the remote run | Remote run keeps going |

Hiding it means: cycle research only through `submit`. Keeping it means: power users can still run the blocking, slash-command path.

Recommendation: hide. The PRD says 6.1.0 replaces blocking cycle execution, and nothing in the tests or docs depends on it. Standalone `web_research_exa` without a cycle is unaffected either way.

The request hash is distinct from the preview artifact hash. Request permission

## Summary

Operator decision (2026-10-12): hide blocking cycle execution behind guided submission. Sixth layer of the pi-exa 6.1.0 stack, stacked on #181.

**Breaking for opted-in cycle callers:** `web_research_exa` with an active cycle and `researchMode: "active"` (or no mode) now surfaces structured conflicts and stale references and then returns `GUIDED_SUBMISSION_REQUIRED` without dispatching. The guided `submit` path with background monitoring is the only normal dispatch. Standalone, default-opt-out and MCP calls are unchanged.

## Changes

- `feat(pi-exa)!`: remove blocking cycle execution. Explicitly funded `retry` / `replace` keep their operator-command consent but dispatch through the same shared non-blocking helper and register monitoring; the blocking agent factory is gone. Completed-on-acknowledgement results carry the execution, completion summary and final report; remote failures and invalid local output remain error results.
- **Bug caught while porting:** a dialog approval could be persisted for a submission that was then refused because the cycle already held an attempt. Guided `submit` now refuses that before any dialog, so no approval is recorded for a refused submission.
- Foundation regressions ported from command-funded blocking execution to dialog-approved submission; monitor-driven GETs are awaited where tests inspect GET counts.

## Note on retry/replace funding

The dialog grants exactly the estimate as the lifetime ceiling. '''## Known prototype simplifications

The prototype is design evidence for host capabilities, not a model of the production
store. A 2026-10-12 review recorded these deliberate gaps; the production implementation
(#172–#174) addresses each of them and the prototype is not maintained further:

- The prototype store is one JSON file rewritten whole without a lock or merge, and its
  attempt IDs are counter-based; an unreadable file is replaced by an empty store.
  Production uses the private, locked, validated per-cycle controller.
- Proposal consumption is checked before the dialog only, so parallel submits of one
  proposal could each create. Production rechecks inside the approval write and refuses
  a second attempt.
- A GET in flight across `session_shutdown` can finish its tick, and timer callbacks do
  not catch storage errors. Production fences ticks by monitor identity and pauses on
  storage failure.
- Every create rejection is classified unknown, and a late acknowledgement racing the
  deadline can be left unmonitored. Production keeps the conservative unknown rule but
  adopts genuine late acknowledgements into background monitoring.
- Acknowledgement is observed only on `agent_settled`, with no `uncertain` state.
  Production also acknowledges at session start and marks sent-but-unconfirmed notices
  uncertain.

## Unsupported guarantees (explicit)''')])

'''### Lifecycle fences''',
'''### Review hardening (2026-10-12)

- Notices are claimed with a serialized `pending → sent` write before `sendMessage`, so a
  monitor tick and an explicit resume cannot both deliver one notice; a failed send
  releases the claim. A re-sent uncertain notice keeps a persisted `possibleDuplicate`
  label until it is delivered.
- A terminal outcome returned in a foreground tool result (explicit recover, or an
  acknowledgement that is already terminal) is never notified again: resume only reports
  terminal attempts that a background monitor owned, and recover acknowledges an existing
  monitor's notice with `channel: "tool-result"`.
- A genuine create acknowledgement that arrives after `SUBMISSION_UNKNOWN` (including an
  unknown original after a replacement) is adopted into background monitoring.
- Dialog approvals merge with the grant current at write time (never lowering a ceiling
  or scope), recheck for an existing attempt inside the write, and are not offered while
  overspend, conflicting receipts or unassessed unknown liabilities exist.
- Provider/contact requests have no package estimate: the operator assesses the exact
  request by command and the dialog confirms that existing funding.
- Monitors detach only on non-cancellable events (`session_shutdown`, `session_tree`); a
  vetoed switch or fork keeps observing. Ticks act only for the live entry of their key.

### Lifecycle fences''')])

## Summary

All production findings are fixed here, at the top of the stack, against the final code; prototype (#176) findings are either fixed (overstated tests) or documented as known prototype limits.

**Package:** `@feniix/pi-exa`.

## Findings → fixes

**#177 / #182 guided consent**
- Submit without an active cycle fell through to a standalone paid Agent run → refused.
- Dialog shown and approval written before feasibility was known; approval could be recorded for a refused submission (also under concurrency) → attempt recheck inside the approval write, submitter preflight before the dialog, `DIALOG_APPROVAL_BLOCKED` for overspend / conflicting receipts / unassessed unknown liabilities (also for the exploration dialog, where a higher-priority scope reason hid them).
- Dialog grants could lower a wider ceiling or scope recorded meanwhile → merged with the grant current at write time.
- Provider/contact requests were funded at the base price → operator-assessed: no package estimate, operator records `approve` + `approve-request`, the dialog confirms.
- `SUBMISSION_NOT_DISPATCHED` told the assistant to submit again (impossible) → points at funded `retry`; a wait expiring before dispatch is now "not dispatched", not "unknown".
- Cycle mismatch reported as `AGENT_ATTEMPT_EXISTS` → mismatch reported first.
- Duplicated create building between lifecycles; dead `agentObserver`; per-call dispatch closure; redundant reads → shared builder, option removed, hoisted helper, terminal path reuses its snapshot.

**#179 / #180 / #182 background monitoring**
- Tick and resume could both deliver one notice → serialized claim (`pending → sent`) before sending; failed send releases it.
- Uncertain label lost after a failed re-send → persisted `possibleDuplicate`.
- Resume re-notified runs already reported in a tool result (terminal-on-ack, explicit recover) → resume only reports background-owned attempts; recover acknowledges an existing monitor's notice (`channel: "tool-result"`) and clears paused guidance.
- Late acknowledgement of an unknown original after replacement was never observed → genuine late create acknowledgements are adopted into monitoring.
- Storage failure in the transient branch killed the monitor silently → any storage failure in a tick pauses (`STORAGE`).
- Stale ticks could reschedule or pause a re-registered monitor → ticks act only for the live entry of their key.
- Resume of a dead owner's live monitor kept the old origin and lifetime → taken over by the resuming session.
- One failing attempt aborted the whole resume → per-attempt isolation.
- Vetoed switch/fork paused every monitor → detach only on `session_shutdown` / `session_tree`.
- Start paused other live runtimes' monitors and warned about foreign notices forever → live owners left alone; warnings only for this session's undelivered notices, after acknowledgement.
- First backoff step repeated the initial delay → 5 s, 7.5 s, 11.25 s …; cap never below the initial delay.
- Ack cache never populated; duplicated liveness probe and notice construction; dead code → fixed / shared helpers.

**#181 flags and fixtures**
- Late flags never reached factory-registered tools (timeouts), config-disabled tools stayed registered unwrapped, planner tools split across plans → call-time timeouts, hidden withdrawal, one shared planner.
- Deprecation warning on every call → once. `EXA_BASE_URL` unvalidated → absolute http(s) required.
- Smoke sync point matched old records; `RpcPi.stop` removed files while the child ran; mock counted unexpected GETs as monitoring → fixed.

**#176 prototype** — dedup/backoff tests asserted less than claimed → fixed or claim dropped; the remaining prototype simplifications are listed in the capability research doc.

**Restored coverage from #182**: interrupted-liability recovery regression; exact projection count.

## Accepted residuals (documented in the plan)

- Approval write and attempt reservation are two serialized transactions; a retry landing between them can still leave a recorded approval.
- A late terminal acknowledgement after its cycle detached cannot register a monitor record; the outcome is retained and shown by status, without a notice.
- Owner liveness is pid-based; pid reuse after a crash is the foundation's existing limit.

https://github.com/feniix/pi-extensions/pull/183 is open with all review fixes. All 7 PRs in the stack pass CI at their current heads.

**What got reviewed and fixed**
- All 6 original PRs were reviewed: 59 findings. Every production finding is fixed in #183. The prototype findings were either fixed (two tests claimed more than they checked) or written down as known prototype limits.
- #183 itself was then reviewed: 10 more findings, all fixed with regression tests.

- The approval write and the attempt reservation are separate steps. A retry landing between them can leave an approval saved with no attempt.
- Owner liveness uses process IDs, so a reused process ID after a crash can look alive. This limit predates the stack.

No known bugs from the reviews remain open. CI is green on all 7 PRs, including #183 at `33ef956`.

Fixed this round, all in #183:
- **Approval without an attempt.** The dialog approval and the Agent reservation are now saved in one write, so a saved approval always has its attempt.
- **Reused process IDs.** Cycle owners and storage locks now also store their process start time. A dead owner whose process ID was reused no longer blocks resume or leaves a lock stuck.
- **Prototype (#176).** I fixed its 7 documented code limits and covered them with tests:
  - The state file is locked and merged before writing, and an unreadable one is set aside instead of overwritten.
  - Two parallel submits of the same proposal now create one run, not two.
  - Monitoring checks that finish after shutdown are ignored, and a failing check pauses instead of crashing.
  - When Exa refuses a create outright, the attempt is marked "rejected", not "unknown".
  - Delivered notices are also recognized at session start.

17	- **Opt-in integrated Pi research cycles** behind `--exa-enable-cycles`, disabled by default. Explicit start/resume connects planning, curated evidence, request previews, approved research, results and accounting. `/exa-research` manages project-isolated durable cycles; session navigation/reload detaches ownership, and reset archives history rather than deleting it or cancelling remote work.
18	- **Versioned, immutable Agent request artifacts** compiled from curated goals, criteria, scope, constraints, selected evidence and a draft-07 structured task contract. Preview and execution share the authoritative request; stale references, conflicting overrides and unsupported schemas fail closed. Explicit input/exclusion rows remain separate from selected source context.
19	- **Operator-issued lifetime ceilings and scoped, one-use permissions.** Exploratory calls reserve exposure before dispatch; Agent research additionally requires an exact full-request assessment. Unknown liabilities, pending estimates, API-reported receipts and overspend are classified separately. Assistant flags, readiness, healthy accounting and supplied amounts never establish spending consent.
20	- **Metadata-first evidence candidates** from cycle-attributed retrievals, with stable URL identities, retrieval state and operation provenance. Selection/rejection and candidate/external-source curation are explicit; only selected source context enters compiled requests and brief/source-pack summaries. Discovery never automatically selects evidence or satisfies criteria.
21	- **Durable Agent submission intent and one-use dispatch claims**, with final ownership, generation, request, history and funding checks before SDK create. Curated results retain validated task output, safe citation metadata, usage and package-owned diagnostics. Genuine late outcomes reconcile their original attempts, including after archival; remote success closes the cycle even when local processing fails.
22	- **Explicit saved-cycle resume and existing-run recovery** through status `action: "resume"` and Agent `researchMode: "recover"`. Recovery performs one bounded GET against the saved run and original frozen contract, without a new submission, reservation, polling loop or remote cancellation. Missing IDs and unavailable inspection preserve unknown work.
23	- **Explicitly funded retry and replacement** through Agent `researchMode: "retry"` / `"replace"`. Each new attempt needs fresh exact-request funding; every unknown original additionally needs operator `approve-replacement` acknowledging duplicate work and possible additional charges. Historical contracts, consumed permissions and liabilities remain intact; genuine completion blocks further submissions and duplicate successes remain visible.
24	- **Guided research from request through approved submission** (6.1.0, #172). `exa_research_status` `action: "start"` creates a non-spending cycle conversationally; `exa_research_summary` `mode: "proposal"` renders the readable scope/cost proposal and its `proposalId`; `web_research_exa` `researchMode: "submit"` asks the operator through Pi's confirmation dialog, records the lifetime scope/ceiling and one-use exact-request permission in one durable write, performs one bounded create and returns the saved Exa run ID while the job is still pending. Stale proposals, declined/dismissed/timed-out dialogs, headless modes and missing estimates fail closed and submit nothing; an unacknowledged create stays unknown and saves a genuine late run ID without resubmitting. Optional exploratory retrieval is disclosed and approved through the same dialog. New `--exa-submit-timeout-ms` flag (default 30000).
25	- **Background monitoring and completion delivery** (6.1.0, #173). Approved submissions register a host-owned monitor that observes only the saved run with bounded, non-overlapping GETs (first after 5 s, ×1.5 backoff to 60 s with jitter; pauses after 8 transient failures or 10 min of silence, immediately on auth/not-found, and after 3 h). Monitoring has no create, retry, replace or cancel authority and runs only while Pi is open. Terminal facts, classified usage and the local validation outcome are persisted before one completion notice per attempt is recorded and delivered to the originating session through Pi's message queue (`exa-research-completion`), acknowledged by observing the persisted session entry. Shutdown, switch, fork, tree navigation and archive pause monitors; restart surfaces stale monitors and pending or uncertain notices without delivering them elsewhere. Registration failure after a create still returns the saved run ID with monitoring paused. New `--exa-monitor-interval-ms` flag (default 5000).
26	- **Monitoring and notification recovery across interruptions** (6.1.0, #174). Shutdown preserves run IDs, frozen contracts, grants, liabilities, monitor intent and notice state; restart discovers them without ownership, submission or monitoring, pausing only monitors whose owner is absent or proven dead. Explicit resume reacquires ownership, re-registers eligible paused monitors for the existing saved run, creates the notice missing after a scheduling crash and delivers pending or uncertain notices into the resuming session (re-sent notices are labeled possible duplicates; exactly-once is not claimed). Competing live runtimes are refused; late original facts settle after archive without reactivating monitoring or delivering into the archived context.
27	- **Offline qualification of the complete guided journey** (6.1.0, #175). Guided background research for Pi. Behind the opt-in `--exa-enable-cycles` flag, a user can ask for research in plain language, approve a readable scope/cost proposal in Pi's own confirmation dialog, keep chatting while the Exa Agent run executes, and get a completion report when it finishes. Standalone, default-opt-out and MCP behavior are unchanged.

### Added

- **Guided research from request to approved submission** (#172). `exa_research_status` `action: "start"` creates a non-spending cycle conversationally; `exa_research_summary` `mode: "proposal"` renders the readable proposal (question, scope and exclusions, criteria, assumptions, source strategy, deliverable, effort, providers, estimate and basis, lifetime allowance, existing liabilities) with a `proposalId` bound to the exact compiled request; `web_research_exa` `researchMode: "submit"` asks the operator through Pi's confirmation dialog and returns the saved Exa run ID while the job is still pending. Stale proposals, declined/dismissed/timed-out dialogs, headless modes, missing estimates, overspend, conflicting receipts and unassessed unknown liabilities submit nothing. Requests with Exa Connect providers are operator-assessed by command and confirmed by the dialog. An unacknowledged create stays unknown; a genuine late acknowledgement is saved on the original attempt and monitored. Optional exploratory retrieval is disclosed and approved through the same dialog.
- **Background monitoring and completion delivery** (#173). Each approved run gets a host-owned monitor that observes only that run with bounded, non-overlapping GETs (first after 5 s, then ×1.5 backoff up to 60 s with jitter); it pauses after 8 transient failures or 10 minutes of silence, immediately on authentication, not-found or configuration errors, and after 3 hours. Monitoring has no create, retry, replace or cancel authority and runs only while Pi is open. Terminal facts, classified usage and local validation are persisted first; then one completion notice per attempt is claimed and delivered to the originating session through Pi's message queue (`exa-research-completion`) and acknowledged by observing the persisted session entry. Outcomes already reported in a tool result are never notified again.
- **Recovery across interruptions** (#174). Shutdown preserves run IDs, frozen contracts, grants, liabilities, monitor intent and notice state; restart discovers them without taking ownership. An explicit conversational resume reacquires ownership, re-registers paused monitors for the existing run, creates any notice lost to a crash and delivers pending or uncertain notices (re-sent notices are labeled possible duplicates; exactly-once delivery is not claimed). Live runtimes elsewhere are never taken over; dead owners are detected by pid and process start time, so a reused pid does not block recovery. Session switch, fork, tree navigation and archive fence monitoring and delivery; a vetoed switch or fork does not.
- **Durable, opt-in Pi research cycles** behind `--exa-enable-cycles`. Project-isolated private records connect planning, curated evidence, versioned compiled Agent requests (draft-07 task contract, selected evidence kept separate from input/exclusion rows), accounting and results. Operator-issued lifetime ceilings and one-use permissions gate every paid call; unknown liabilities, pending estimates, API-reported receipts and overspend are classified separately, and assistant-supplied flags or amounts never grant consent. Cycle-attributed retrievals capture metadata-only evidence candidates that are selected explicitly. `/exa-research` remains available for start, list, resume, explicit approvals and archive.
- **Explicit recovery, retry and replacement.** `researchMode: "recover"` performs one bounded GET of an existing saved run; `"retry"` and `"replace"` need fresh operator funding (and `approve-replacement` for every unknown original) and dispatch through the same non-blocking path with background monitoring. Genuine completion blocks further submissions; duplicate successes stay visible with their separate costs.
- **Read-only final cycle reports** with recorded criteria, evidence-reference diagnostics, gaps, assumptions, completion facts and classified usage. Generated claims never satisfy criteria automatically.
- **New options:** `--exa-submit-timeout-ms` (create acknowledgement wait, default 30000), `--exa-monitor-interval-ms` (first background check, default 5000) and the `EXA_BASE_URL` environment variable for a self-hosted proxy or endpoint mock (absolute http(s) URL required).
- **Offline qualification** (#171, #175). PRD-010 scenarios 1–36 map to executable evidence, including a production smoke that drives the real extension in a real `pi --mode rpc` process against a controllable mock Exa server, plus a recorded interactive TUI run. Host capability research for Pi 1.1.0 is in `docs/research/2026-10-12-pi-guided-background-host-capabilities.md`.

     - (a) the approval write and the attempt reservation were separate transactions (now fixed);
     - (b) pid-reuse owner liveness (in progress);

     - No version bump, release, tag or publish without separate authorization.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - gh-stack: `gh stack add/checkout/rebase --upstack/push/submit --auto --open/view --json`. Merge with `gh stack merge <pr> --yes`.
   - Pi 1.1.0 extension API:

     - Events: `agent_settled`, `session_start`, `session_shutdown` (reasons quit/reload/new/resume/fork), `session_tree`.
     - Flags are registered by bare name and applied after factories run.
     - Re-registering a tool with `exposure:"hidden"` withdraws it.
   - Cycle controller (research-cycles.ts): transactions, `owned()`, `write()` with atomic rename, `activate`, `ordered`, grants/ledger/attempts, `agentLifecycleObserver`, `prepareAgentRecovery`.
   - Monitor runtime in cycle-pi.ts:

     - `stopWithNotice` helper;

3. Files and Code Sections:

     - grantBudget gains a `source` parameter and merges dialog grants.
     - Latest change: reserveAgent's body was extracted into `prepareAgentReservation(record, reference, transitionMode)`, which mutates in memory and sets `record.status="running"`. reserveAgent now calls it and writes once.
     - `grantDialogApproval` was replaced by `approveAndReserveAgent(cycleId, approval)`. Inside one transaction it:
       1. checks for an existing attempt (AGENT_ATTEMPT_EXISTS, checked first);
       2. checks the artifact target and artifact hash (PROPOSAL_STALE);

       ```ts
       export function ownerAlive(owner: { pid: number; processStart?: string } | undefined): boolean {
         if (!owner) return false;
         try { process.kill(owner.pid, 0); } catch (error) { return code(error) !== "ESRCH"; }
         if (owner.processStart === undefined) return true;
         const current = processStartTime(owner.pid);
         return current === undefined || current === owner.processStart;
       }
       export function processStartTime(pid: number): string | undefined {
         if (process.platform === "win32") return undefined;
         try { const value = execFileSync("ps", ["-o","lstart=","-p",String(pid)], {encoding:"utf8",stdio:["ignore","pipe","ignore"],timeout:2_000}).trim();
           return value ? value.replace(/\s+/g, " ") : undefined; } catch { return undefined; }
       }
       const ownProcessStart = processStartTime(process.pid);
       const owner = { sessionId: options.sessionId, token: randomUUID(), pid: process.pid, ...(ownProcessStart === undefined ? {} : { processStart: ownProcessStart }) };
       ```

content.text: There are 99 user-facing commits since 6.0.2, and my rewrite dropped detail from several. The new 6.1.0 section combines the original running entries with the summaries, so every change is covered.

input.command:
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='packages/pi-exa/CHANGELOG.md'
s=open(p).read()
start=s.index('## [6.1.0] - 2026-10-12')
end=s.index('## [6.0.2] - 2026-10-06')
section='''## [6.1.0] - 2026-10-12

Guided background research for Pi, built on new opt-in durable research cycles. Behind `--exa-enable-cycles`, a user can ask for research in plain language, approve a readable scope/cost proposal in Pi's own confirmation dialog, keep chatting while the Exa Agent run executes, and get a completion report when it finishes. Standalone, default-opt-out and MCP behavior are unchanged.

### Added

- **Opt-in integrated Pi research cycles** behind `--exa-enable-cycles`, disabled by default. Explicit start/resume connects planning, curated evidence, request previews, approved research, results and accounting. `/exa-research` manages project-isolated durable cycles; session navigation/reload detaches ownership, and reset archives history rather than deleting it or cancelling remote work.
- **Versioned, immutable Agent request artifacts** compiled from curated goals, criteria, scope, constraints, selected evidence and a draft-07 structured task contract. Preview and execution share the authoritative request; stale references, conflicting overrides and unsupported schemas fail closed. Explicit input/exclusion rows remain separate from selected source context.
- **Operator-issued lifetime ceilings and scoped, one-use permissions.** Exploratory calls reserve exposure before dispatch using published contents and advanced-search rates; Agent research additionally requires an exact full-request assessment. Unknown liabilities, pending estimates, API-reported receipts and overspend are classified separately. Assistant flags, readiness, healthy accounting and supplied amounts never establish spending consent.
- **Metadata-first evidence candidates** from cycle-attributed retrievals, with stable URL identities, retrieval state and operation provenance. Selection/rejection and candidate/external-source curation are explicit; only selected source context enters compiled requests and brief/source-pack summaries. Discovery never automatically selects evidence or satisfies criteria.
- **Durable Agent submission intent and one-use dispatch claims**, with final ownership, generation, request, history and funding checks before SDK create. Curated results retain validated task output, safe citation metadata, usage and package-owned diagnostics. Genuine late outcomes reconcile their original attempts, including after archival; remote success closes the cycle even when local processing fails.
- **Explicit saved-cycle resume and existing-run recovery** through status `action: "resume"` and Agent `researchMode: "recover"`. Recovery performs one bounded GET against the saved run and original frozen contract, without a new submission, reservation, polling loop or remote cancellation. Missing IDs and unavailable inspection preserve unknown work.
- **Explicitly funded retry and replacement** through Agent `researchMode: "retry"` / `"replace"`. Each new attempt needs fresh exact-request funding; every unknown original additionally needs operator `approve-replacement` acknowledging duplicate work and possible additional charges. Historical contracts, consumed permissions and liabilities remain intact; genuine completion blocks further submissions and duplicate successes remain visible.
- **Guided research from request to approved submission** (#172). `exa_research_status` `action: "start"` creates a non-spending cycle conversationally; `exa_research_summary` `mode: "proposal"` renders the readable proposal (question, scope and exclusions, criteria, assumptions, source strategy, deliverable, effort, providers, estimate and basis, lifetime allowance, existing liabilities) with a `proposalId` bound to the exact compiled request; `web_research_exa` `researchMode: "submit"` asks the operator through Pi's confirmation dialog and returns the saved Exa run ID while the job is still pending. Stale proposals, declined/dismissed/timed-out dialogs, headless modes and missing estimates fail closed and submit nothing; an unacknowledged create stays unknown and saves a genuine late run ID without resubmitting. Optional exploratory retrieval is disclosed and approved through the same dialog.
- **Background monitoring and completion delivery** (#173). Approved submissions register a host-owned monitor that observes only the saved run with bounded, non-overlapping GETs (first after 5 s, then ×1.5 backoff to 60 s with jitter; pauses after 8 transient failures or 10 min of silence, immediately on authentication, not-found or configuration errors, and after 3 h). Monitoring has no create, retry, replace or cancel authority and runs only while Pi is open. Terminal facts, classified usage and the local validation outcome are persisted before one completion notice per attempt is recorded and delivered to the originating session through Pi's message queue (`exa-research-completion`), acknowledged by observing the persisted session entry. Registration failure after a create still returns the saved run ID with monitoring paused.
- **Monitoring and notification recovery across interruptions** (#174). Shutdown preserves run IDs, frozen contracts, grants, liabilities, monitor intent and notice state; restart discovers them without ownership, submission or monitoring, pausing only monitors whose owner is absent or proven dead. Explicit resume reacquires ownership, re-registers eligible paused monitors for the existing saved run, creates the notice missing after a scheduling crash and delivers pending or uncertain notices into the resuming session (re-sent notices are labeled possible duplicates; exactly-once is not claimed). Competing live runtimes are refused; late original facts settle after archive without reactivating monitoring or delivering into the archived context.
- **Read-only final cycle reports** with recorded criteria, evidence-reference diagnostics, gaps, assumptions, completion facts and classified usage. Integrated tool guidance and the planner skill describe the Pi workflow.
- **New options:** `--exa-submit-timeout-ms` (create acknowledgement wait, default 30000), `--exa-monitor-interval-ms` (first background check, default 5000) and the `EXA_BASE_URL` environment variable for a self-hosted proxy or endpoint mock (absolute http(s) URL required).
- **Offline qualification of the complete guided journey** (#175). A production smoke drives the real extension in a real `pi --mode rpc` process with the real `exa-js` SDK pointed at a controllable mock Exa HTTP server: request → draft → readable proposal → trusted approval over the protocol → immediate saved run ID → continued conversation → background completion → report, plus a cancelled-dialog journey and a recorded interactive TUI run. The qualification document maps PRD-010 scenarios 1–36 to executable evidence and states what remains unclaimed.

### Changed

- **Blocking cycle execution is removed.** `web_research_exa` with an active cycle and `researchMode: "active"` (or no mode) now returns `GUIDED_SUBMISSION_REQUIRED` after surfacing structured conflicts and stale references; the guided `submit` path with background monitoring is the only normal dispatch. Explicitly funded `retry` / `replace` keep their operator-command consent but dispatch through the same non-blocking path and register monitoring. Standalone, default-opt-out and MCP `web_research_exa` calls keep their existing blocking behavior.
- **Coalesce unchanged Agent observations and reuse status projections**, avoiding redundant record rewrites and repeated storage-hierarchy synchronization while preserving changed/late usage, results, conflicting receipts and durability repair.
- Target Pi 1.1.0 (`@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`, `pi-ai`, `pi-tui`); the guided background workflow uses the latest Pi 1.x extension API.
- Add `ajv` and `ajv-formats` for synchronous local draft-07 task/result validation; validation does not fetch remote schemas.
- Settle the guided background host contract (#171): proposal-bound `submit` approval through the Pi confirmation dialog, bounded create acknowledgement, non-overlapping monitor cadence/backoff and pause limits, and completion delivery acknowledged by the persisted session entry. Evidence lives in `docs/research/2026-10-12-pi-guided-background-host-capabilities.md` and the prototype experiments under `__tests__/fixtures/guided-prototype/`; the prototype's own store safety and race gaps found in review are fixed too.
- Estimates and lifetime ceilings are not vendor billing caps, and SDK receipts are not independently verified invoices. Cycle `max`/`ultra` and MCP cycle parity remain outside this rollout.

### Fixed

- **Extension CLI flags are reachable by their documented names.** Pi registers flags by bare name and the CLI strips the leading dashes itself, so the `--exa-*` registrations were only reachable as `----exa-*`. `--exa-api-key`, `--exa-enable-advanced`, `--exa-enable-research`, `--exa-config-file`, `--exa-config`, `--exa-timeout-ms`, `--exa-research-timeout-ms`, `--exa-submit-timeout-ms` and `--exa-monitor-interval-ms` now parse as documented.
- **Flags applied after the factory now take effect everywhere.** Pi applies flag values only after extension factories run, so tool enablement from `--exa-config-file`, `--exa-enable-advanced` and `--exa-enable-research` is refreshed at `session_start`, registering newly enabled tools and withdrawing (hiding) newly disabled ones. Tool timeouts are resolved at call time, the four planner tools share one plan across registrations, and the `--exa-config` deprecation warning prints once.
- **Guided consent hardening (review).** `researchMode: "submit"` without an active cycle is refused instead of running a standalone paid Agent call; a mismatched `cycleId` is reported before anything about the active cycle; the dialog is not offered while overspend, conflicting receipts or unassessed unknown liabilities exist (`DIALOG_APPROVAL_BLOCKED`); a cycle that already holds a saved attempt is refused before any dialog; dialog grants merge with the grant current at write time instead of lowering a wider ceiling or scope; a missing submitter is detected before the dialog. Provider/contact requests are no longer funded at the base price: the operator assesses the exact request by command and the dialog confirms it. A wait that expires before the create is sent is reported as not dispatched (no charge) with the explicit retry path.
- **Atomic dialog approval.** The lifetime grant, the one-use exact-request permission and the frozen attempt are written in one durable transaction, so an approval is never recorded without its attempt and any reservation failure writes nothing.
- **Background monitoring hardening (review).** Notices are claimed before sending so a tick and a resume cannot both deliver one; a failed re-send keeps its possible-duplicate label; foreground-reported terminal outcomes are recorded and never notified again on resume, while a late acknowledgement that arrived after detach is still notified; genuine late create acknowledgements are adopted into monitoring; storage failures anywhere in a tick pause the monitor; stale ticks never act for a re-registered monitor; a resumed dead owner's monitor moves to the resuming session; resume isolates per-attempt failures; monitors no longer pause on a vetoed switch or fork; another live runtime's monitors and notices are left alone at session start, and other sessions' undelivered notices are summarized; the first backoff step now follows the first check (5 s, then 7.5 s); an invalid `EXA_BASE_URL` pauses monitoring as a configuration error.
- **Pid reuse no longer hides a dead owner.** Cycle owners and storage locks record their process start time, so a pid reused after a crash no longer makes a dead owner look alive, block resume or leave a lock stuck. Records without a start time keep the conservative pid-only rule.
- **Replacement liability guards reuse the complete shared attempt floor**, including known receipt conflicts and the immutable fixed-effort base, instead of re-deriving a partial floor. Stale replacement consent is rejected before reservation without consuming permissions or changing saved history.
- **Exact conservative decimal micro-USD conversion** avoids binary floating-point boundary errors when flooring permission or ceiling exposure. Equivalent known terminal SDK receipts retain legitimate historical rounding without creating false conflicts; genuinely changed receipts remain auditable.
- **Storage and ownership availability:** atomically published PID/token transaction locks recover only proven-dead owners, use monotonic bounded contention waits and clean candidate links. Unverifiable/live locks are retained with actionable repair paths. Archiving unrelated history no longer revokes the active cycle, and readable discovery survives corrupt records while continuation attribution stays fail-closed.
- **Standalone isolation and selected-only summaries:** explicit unrelated standalone retrieval bypasses owned-cycle status failures without bypassing saved-run attribution, and contradictory standalone cycle references are rejected. Shared summary projection prevents drift, and final-report diagnostics match the evidence visible in each view without changing saved criteria or exposing unselected source notes.

### Security

- Keep durable cycle state private and outside git. Automatic retention excludes raw source bodies, full SDK responses, invalid generated output and arbitrary vendor error prose; credential-bearing/signed URLs and Agent path dot segments are rejected; an invalid `EXA_BASE_URL` is never echoed in errors. Explicit curated notes/rows and requested structured task outputs must remain nonsecret.
- Patch shared transitive dependencies through workspace overrides: `proxy-addr` 2.0.8, `source-map-js` 1.2.2 and `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.31.0. This clears the recorded dependency advisories without changing the frozen Pi, Exa or bridgekit versions.

'''
s=s[:start]+section+s[end:]
open(p,'w').write(s)
PYEOF

 # Laya vs Jev for typed decisions

 ## Bottom line

 Jev is the better starting hypothesis for varied, zero-shot semantic decisions. Laya is worth evaluating for local/private inference, small fixed decision
 spaces, or a domain where you can fine-tune and calibrate a specialist. This is a recommendation from published evidence, not a benchmark run in this
 repository.

 Both return Choice (closed-set selection), Score (ordinal judgment), and Noul (probability of yes), rather than generated prose. Neither replaces
 deterministic authorization or a general reasoning model. Sources: [Laya
 README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ccjjfdyqlhy/laya/refs/heads/main/README.md), [Jev Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md), [Jev
 limitations](https://docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13.md).

 ## Practical differences

 ... (45 more lines, 55 total, ctrl+o to expand)


 Jev is the stronger default for general decisions; Laya is more compelling for local, specialized decisions. Both return typed choices, ordinal scores, and
 yes/no probabilities—not generated explanations.

 ┌────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Difference     │ Laya                                                                  │ Jev                                             │
 ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Deployment     │ Open weights, Apache-2.0; self-hostable                               │ Closed, managed API                             │
 ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Best fit       │ Narrow tasks you can fine-tune                                        │ Varied questions without training               │
 ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Choice options │ Recommended roughly under 20 at default settings                      │ Up to 255                                       │
 ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Context        │ Published checkpoints: 512–1,024 tokens; configurable runtime budgets │ 32k state + longest question; 64k total request │
 ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Customization  │ Fine-tuning and calibration                                           │ Instructions, criteria, and state               │
 ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Cost           │ Infrastructure and operations                                         │ $0.042/million input tokens; output free        │
 └────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

 Sources: Laya documentation, Jev models, Jev choices.

 ### The important benchmark catch

 Laya’s specialist reports 76.6% accuracy versus Jev’s published 72.7%, but:
 - Laya was fine-tuned on that benchmark’s training split.
 - Untuned Laya scored only 34–36%.
 - Jev had better probability-distribution matching and lower calibration error.
 - The publisher explicitly says this was not a controlled head-to-head.

 So “Laya beats Jev” is too broad. The evidence supports “a tuned Laya specialist can outperform published Jev results on its target workflows.” Model card

 ### My recommendation

 For decisions such as source relevance, evidence sufficiency, or routing, I’d start with Jev, then benchmark Laya if local processing or customization
 matters.

 For spending approval, permissions, accounting, or retry authorization, use neither as the authority: keep those rules deterministic. Confidence summarizes
 a model’s distribution—not permission or guaranteed correctness. Jev confidence

The guided flow did not start. #184 should not merge yet, because 6.1.0 would ship a flow that a real model does not pick on its own.

**Why it did not start.** There are three causes, and the first two are enough on their own:
1. **No Agent research tool.** `--exa-enable-cycles` does not enable `web_research_exa`, which needs `--exa-enable-research` or a config file. Without it, the guided `submit` step does not exist in the session. Nothing warns about this at startup.
2. **The trigger is too narrow.** The cycle guidance says to start a cycle "when the user asks for guided research". Its first line also says standalone web tools remain available. A plain request like "research the differences between laya and jev" therefore reads as standalone, and the model did ordinary searches and fetches.
3. **The skill is conditional.** `exa-research-planner` loaded, but its cycle section applies only "when `--exa-enable-cycles` is enabled". The model cannot see flags, so it skipped that branch.

**Why tests did not catch it.** The RPC smoke and the qualification runs use a scripted fake model that calls the cycle tools directly. They prove the approval, monitoring and delivery plumbing, but not that a real model chooses that flow. The qualification document overstates this for the conversational trigger.

**Proposed fix**, about 1 to 2 hours plus a manual retest:
1. Make cycles usable on their own. Either enabling cycles also enables `web_research_exa` for cycle use, or session start warns that guided submission is unavailable.
2. Rewrite the trigger. When cycles are enabled, a request to research a question should start a guided cycle, or offer one in a line. Standalone tools remain for quick lookups or when the user declines.
3. Remove the flag condition from the skill. Tool presence becomes the signal: if `exa_research_status` accepts `action: "start"`, use the guided flow.
4. Retest your exact prompt in Herdr with a real model. Then state honestly in the qualification document that model-choice behavior is checked manually, not automatically.

Separately, the model wrote `docs/research/laya-vs-jev-decisions.md` into the repo. That file is untracked on the release branch. I left it alone.

what does enable-cycles do?

`--exa-enable-cycles` turns the in-memory research planner into durable, spend-controlled research cycles. It does not enable any paid tool by itself.

**What the flag adds:**
1. **Durable cycles.** The `exa_research_*` planning tools save to private files on disk, one set per project, instead of memory. Plans survive restarts.
2. **The `/exa-research` command.** It starts, lists, resumes and archives cycles, and records the operator's spending approvals.
3. **New tool actions.**
   - `exa_research_status` gains `start` and `resume`.
   - `exa_research_summary` gains a readable `proposal` mode.
   - `web_research_exa` gains `submit`, `recover`, `retry` and `replace` modes.
4. **Cycle-aware web tools.** Search and fetch calls made inside a cycle are charged against its budget. Their results become evidence candidates the model can select.
5. **Background machinery.**
   - Approved Agent runs get a host-owned monitor.
   - Completion notices arrive in the session.
   - Session switch, fork, restart and resume each have their own handling.

**What it does not change:**
- Which web tools exist. Search, fetch, answer and find-similar are always on. Advanced search needs `--exa-enable-advanced`. Agent research (`web_research_exa`) needs `--exa-enable-research`.
- Standalone use. Without an active cycle, every tool behaves as in 6.0.2.

So with only `--exa-enable-cycles`, a cycle can be planned and given evidence, but nothing can submit it for Agent research. That is cause 1 from before.

Next: say "fix it" to make `--exa-enable-cycles` alone enough for the guided flow.

 # Laya vs Jev for decisions

 ## Bottom line

 Recommendation (synthesis, not a measured result): use Jev as the initial baseline for general, zero-shot semantic decisions. Evaluate Laya for bounded,
 short-input decisions when local deployment, open weights, or domain fine-tuning are important. Neither model's typed output guarantees a correct decision
 or authorizes an action.

 This research reviewed public documentation and published benchmarks; it did not execute either model or spend on inference. Laya Studio is an independent
 hosting company, not the Laya model's author. Its comparison is useful context, not independent validation. [1–7]

 ## Practical differences

 ... (75 more lines, 85 total, ctrl+o to expand)


 Jev is the stronger starting point for general decisions; Laya is more attractive for local, specialized decisions.

 Both return typed choices, scores, and yes/no probabilities—not prose explanations.

 ┌────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Difference     │ Jev                                           │ Laya                                                    │
 ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Deployment     │ Proprietary hosted API                        │ Open weights, self-hostable, fine-tunable               │
 ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Context        │ Up to 32k tokens for state + longest question │ Defaults to 512–1,024 tokens including question/options │
 ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Choices        │ Supports up to 255 options                    │ Best kept around 20 or fewer                            │
 ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Adaptation     │ Instructions and supplied context             │ Instructions, fine-tuning, calibration                  │
 ├────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Main advantage │ Generality, larger inputs and label sets      │ Deployment control and specialization                   │
 └────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

 Sources: Jev documentation, Laya maintainer guidance.

 ### The important benchmark caveat

 Laya’s specialist reports 76.6% accuracy versus Jev’s 72.7%, but it was trained specifically for that benchmark. Base Laya scored 36.2%, below the
 majority-class baseline. Jev had better reported calibration and soft accuracy.

 These results aren’t a controlled head-to-head: the Laya authors imported Jev’s numbers from another evaluation. Benchmark details

 ### My recommendation

 - General agent routing and semantic checks: start with Jev.
 - Short, repeatable decisions with training data or local-deployment requirements: evaluate Laya.
 - Approval, spending, or destructive actions: keep authorization in deterministic code. Neither model’s confidence constitutes consent.

 Also, don’t transfer confidence thresholds between them—their formulas differ. Laya’s advertised speed advantage compares local GPU inference against Jev
 HTTP latency, so benchmark your actual deployment.

Start Pi with `--exa-enable-cycles` to use durable research planning.

The normal path needs no slash commands, copied hashes or hand-written schemas.
Say what you want researched; the assistant drives the cycle and you make the
material decisions through Pi's own confirmation dialog:

1. **Draft.** The assistant starts a non-spending cycle with

   scope/cost proposal: question, scope and exclusions, criteria, assumptions,
   source strategy, deliverable, effort, providers, input/exclusion rows,
   estimated cost and basis, lifetime allowance and existing liabilities. It
   returns a `proposalId` bound to that exact compiled request and revision.
3. **Approval.** `web_research_exa` `researchMode: "submit"` with the active

- `exa_research_*` planning tools are enabled by default when no explicit `enabledTools` allowlist is configured, local-only, and do not require an Exa API key.
